title: Mutabbal
description: Mutabbal is a Levantine dip of roasted, mashed eggplant with tahini, yoghurt, garlic and lemon, and it is a regular side with grilled meat on Saudi tables. Here the eggplant is roasted without coating it in oil, with low-fat yoghurt, less tahini and only a drizzle of olive oil.
ingredients: 2 tbsp lemon juice (30 g) and 2 tsp white vinegar (10 g)
1 tsp olive oil to drizzle (4.5 g)
Lemon slices, parsley and a pinch of cumin or paprika to garnish
steps: Prick the eggplants with a fork and roast them whole, without oil, in a 220 °C oven (or over a gas flame) for 40–45 minutes, turning, until completely soft and charred.
Let cool a little, peel, and drain the flesh in a sieve for 10 minutes.
Mash the eggplant with a fork or chop it finely with a knife.
Add the garlic, vinegar, lemon juice, yoghurt, tahini and salt and mix with a spoon until even.
Spread it in a serving dish, drizzle the olive oil in a circle, garnish with lemon, parsley and cumin, and serve cold.
hints: What changed: the eggplant is roasted without being coated in oil, only 2 tbsp tahini, low-fat yoghurt, and 1 tsp olive oil on top.
Kidney tip: eggplant, tahini and yoghurt contain potassium and phosphorus; keep to one serving (4 tbsp) and you can cut the tahini to 1 tbsp.
Diabetes tip: mutabbal is low in carbohydrate; watch the bread eaten with it and use cucumber and carrot sticks instead.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Sayidaty

title: Jibniyya
description: Jibniyya is a popular sweet of the Saudi kitchen: a soft yeast dough kneaded with cheese and evaporated milk, cut into rounds, fried and soaked in syrup or honey, then topped with pistachios or almonds. In this version the rounds are baked, with low-fat cream cheese, fat-free evaporated milk and half whole-wheat flour, and a light glaze of honey instead of syrup.
ingredients: 2 tbsp honey (40 g) thinned with 1 tbsp warm water
steps: Mix both flours with the yeast, sugar and salt, then add the cream cheese and evaporated milk and knead, adding the water little by little, to a soft, smooth dough that does not stick to your hands.
Cover the dough and leave to rise for 1 hour or until doubled.
Dust the worktop with a little flour, roll the dough about ½ cm thick and cut 12 rounds with a glass or cutter.
Place the rounds on a tray lined with baking paper, brush with the oil and leave for 15 minutes to puff; heat the oven to 200 °C.
Bake the rounds for 12–15 minutes until puffed and golden.
Brush them while hot with the thinned honey, sprinkle with pistachios and serve warm.
hints: What changed: baked instead of fried, low-fat cream cheese instead of full-fat cheese, fat-free evaporated milk, half whole-wheat flour, and 40 g honey for the whole batch instead of a glass of syrup.
Kidney tip: cheese, evaporated milk and pistachios contain phosphorus; keep to one piece, and you can skip the pistachios and use only white flour.
Diabetes tip: one piece has about 21 g carbohydrate; have one piece without the honey glaze, with Arabic coffee or unsweetened tea.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Saudi cuisine), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Baked Meat Samboosa
description: Samboosa are triangles of thin pastry filled with minced meat, onion and coriander, a fixture of the Ramadan iftar table in Saudi Arabia. This version is baked instead of deep-fried and uses lean meat, little salt and plenty of fresh herbs.
ingredients: ½ bunch fresh coriander, chopped (20 g)
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp cardamom and a pinch of black pepper
1 tbsp flour (5 g) mixed with a little water to seal
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) for brushing
steps: Heat the teaspoon of oil in a non-stick pan and soften the onion, then add the meat and stir until browned and dry.
Add the garlic, chilli, spices and salt and stir for 2 minutes, then take off the heat, add the coriander and parsley and let the filling cool completely.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a tray with baking paper.
Put a spoonful of filling at one end of a pastry strip, fold it over and over into a triangle to the end, and seal the edge with the flour paste.
Arrange the triangles on the tray and brush the tops lightly with the oil.
Bake for 15–18 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crisp, and serve hot.
hints: What changed: baking instead of deep-frying saves most of the fat, with lean meat and less salt.
Kidney tip: ready samboosa pastry contains sodium and the meat contains phosphorus; keep to 4 pieces, and you can replace some of the meat with grated zucchini.
Diabetes tip: 4 pieces have about 21 g carbohydrate; eat them with a vegetable soup or salad rather than adding more pieces.
You can freeze the triangles before baking and bake them straight from frozen, adding 5 minutes.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Saudi cooking book), Sayidaty Kitchen, Arab News, Foodie Atlas

title: Date Aseeda (Muhalla)
description: Date aseeda, also called muhalla, is a Najdi winter sweet of whole-wheat flour and dates slowly cooked with black pepper and warm spices until smooth and sticky, then served with ghee. This version uses about half the traditional amount of dates per gram of flour, a little ghee instead of butter, and a small portion.
ingredients: ½ tsp ground cardamom, ½ tsp cinnamon and ¼ tsp ground ginger
steps: Soak the dates in half the water (hot) for 15 minutes, then blend until smooth.
Toast the flour in a heavy pot over medium heat, stirring, until it colours slightly and smells nutty.
Gradually whisk in the date mixture, the rest of the water, the spices and the salt so no lumps form.
Cook on low heat for at least 1 hour, stirring every 10–15 minutes, until the flour is cooked and the mixture is smooth and glossy.
Divide into 8 small bowls, sprinkle with a little black pepper and drizzle about ¼ tsp ghee on each, and serve warm.
hints: What changed: about half the traditional dates per gram of flour (300 g dates to 150 g flour), no added sugar, a little ghee instead of butter, and a small portion.
Kidney tip: dates and whole-wheat flour contain potassium and phosphorus (about 310 mg potassium per portion); keep to one small bowl and skip the nuts.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 42 g carbohydrate, mostly from the dates; count it as part of the meal's carbs and have it after a meal with protein and vegetables.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad, Sotor

title: Lamb Haneeth
description: Haneeth is a heritage dish of Asir and southern Saudi Arabia: lamb cooked very slowly until it falls apart and served over rice. This oven or pressure-cooker version uses lean, trimmed lamb and little salt.
ingredients: 600 g lamb leg or shoulder, visible fat trimmed (edible weight)
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp turmeric
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
A pinch of saffron soaked in 2 tbsp water
¾ tsp salt (4 g), split between meat and rice
steps: Mix the ground spices, garlic, lemon juice and ¼ tsp of the salt and rub it well into the lamb.
Brush a deep oven dish (or pressure cooker) with the olive oil, spread the onions with the cinnamon, cardamom and cloves on top, then lay the lamb over them.
Seal tightly with foil and cook at 160°C for 3 hours until the lamb falls apart (or 40 minutes after the whistle on low heat in a pressure cooker, with no added water).
Uncover, raise the oven to 220°C and brown the lamb for 10–15 minutes.
Meanwhile boil the water with the ghee and the rest of the salt, add the rice and simmer covered for 15 minutes, then drizzle the saffron on top and rest 5 minutes.
Spread the rice on a platter, arrange the lamb on top and spoon over the cooking juices after skimming off the fat.
Serve with green salad or a light lemony tahini salad.
hints: What changed: trimmed lean lamb instead of fatty cuts, fat skimmed from the juices, measured oil and ghee and much less salt.
Kidney tip: lamb provides phosphorus and potassium; keep to 90–100 g cooked meat and go easy on tahini salad, which is high in phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 48 g carbohydrate; start with the salad and reduce the rice if you need a lighter meal.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), English Wikipedia (Haneeth), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Chicken Maqluba
description: Maqluba is a Levantine dish that is common in Saudi homes: layers of chicken, vegetables and rice are cooked in a pot and turned upside down to serve. In this version the eggplant, potato and zucchini slices are oven-roasted with a little oil instead of fried, with skinless chicken, no stock cubes and limited salt.
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, cut in medium pieces
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black and white pepper, 1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), 3 cardamom pods
1 large eggplant, in 1 cm slices (350 g)
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) to brush the vegetables
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 15 minutes
About 450 ml of the chicken cooking broth (no added salt)
steps: Soak the potato slices in warm water for at least 1 hour, then pat dry (this lowers the potassium). Heat the oven to 220°C.
Brush the eggplant, potato and zucchini slices with the tablespoon of oil, spread them on a lined tray and roast for 20–25 minutes, turning once, until golden.
Meanwhile heat the teaspoon of oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the chicken, garlic and spices and stir for 5 minutes.
Add boiling water to cover the chicken (about 600 ml) and cook for 20 minutes, then strain and keep the broth.
In a deep pot, lay the tomato slices on the bottom, then the chicken, then the roasted vegetables, then the drained rice, and level it.
Dissolve the salt in the hot broth and pour it in gently until it is about 1 cm above the rice, then put a small plate on the rice and bring to the boil; cover and cook on low heat for 25–30 minutes.
Rest for 10 minutes, then put the serving platter on top, turn the pot over firmly and lift it off gently; sprinkle with the parsley. Serve with salad and low-fat yoghurt.
hints: What changed: the vegetables are oven-roasted with one spoon of oil instead of deep-fried, the chicken is skinless, there are no stock cubes, and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: potato, tomato, eggplant and chicken provide potassium and phosphorus; soak the potato as in the first step or swap it for cauliflower, and keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked chicken and 150 g cooked rice). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 60 g carbohydrate from the rice and potato; swap the potato for cauliflower to lower it, and serve with salad.
Suitable for: a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Wikipedia (Maqluba), Sayidaty Kitchen (maqluba with eggplant, cauliflower and potato)

title: Hijazi Purslane Stew
description: Rajla (purslane) stew is a Makkah and Hijazi home dish in which purslane leaves are cooked with chicken or meat, yellow lentils, tomato and spices, and eaten with rice or bread. We used skinless chicken breast, 2 tbsp olive oil instead of about 120 ml oil, and little salt.
ingredients: 500 g skinless chicken breast, cut in small cubes
1 tbsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp cumin
400 g fresh purslane, leaves and tender stems, washed and chopped
Juice of ½ lemon to serve
steps: Boil the lentils in 500 ml water for about 20 minutes until tender, then drain and keep the cooking water.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion and garlic over medium heat until soft but not browned.
Add the chicken and spices and stir until the chicken changes colour and its juices are absorbed.
Add the tomato and cook for 5 minutes until it breaks down, then add the cooked lentils.
Add the purslane and salt, stir, cover and cook on low heat for 10–15 minutes; if it gets dry add a little of the lentil water.
Squeeze over the lemon and serve with whole-wheat bread or a small portion of rice.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken breast, 2 tbsp olive oil instead of about 120 ml vegetable oil, and less salt with no stock cubes.

Kidney tip: purslane is very high in potassium and oxalate, and lentils are high in potassium and phosphorus; boil the purslane for 5 minutes and throw away the water before adding it, halve the lentils, and have half a portion if you must limit potassium.
Diabetes tip: the stew alone has about 26 g carbohydrate; if you add rice keep it to half a portion (about 75 g cooked) or use whole-wheat bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Cookpad, Food2Mins

title: Kebab Mero
description: Kebab mero is a popular street dish from Makkah in the Hijaz: small balls of minced meat, millet flour, onion and spices, usually deep-fried and served with tahini salad. This version uses extra-lean mince, bakes or air-fries the balls instead of frying them, and uses less salt and tahini.
serving_size: about 10 small balls with salad (300 g)
ingredients: 1 medium onion, grated and squeezed (100 g)
½ tsp ground coriander and ¼ tsp ground cardamom
2 tsp olive oil for brushing (10 g)
4 tsp lemon juice (20 g) and 2 tsp vinegar (10 g)
1 pinch salt (1 g), cumin and black pepper
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C, line a tray with baking paper and brush it with half the oil.
Knead the meat with the millet flour, onion, garlic, egg, spices and salt until the mixture holds together.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into small walnut-sized balls (about 40) and set them on the tray.
Brush the balls with the rest of the oil and bake for 12–15 minutes, turning once, until browned outside and still juicy inside, or air-fry at 200 °C for 10–12 minutes.
For the salad: whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, vinegar and a little water to a thin sauce, then add the salt, cumin, pepper, cucumber and tomato.
Serve the kebab hot with the tahini salad.
hints: What changed: extra-lean mince, baking or air-frying instead of deep frying, no stock cubes, and less salt and tahini.
Kidney tip: the meat, tahini and millet flour contain phosphorus and the tomato adds potassium; keep to one portion (10 balls) and you can replace the tomato with more cucumber.
Diabetes tip: one portion has only about 19 g carbohydrate; serve it with green salad and half a wholemeal flatbread instead of white rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Hia Magazine, Al Sayaha Al Arabia

title: Hijazi Lahoh
description: Hijazi lahoh is a thin, spongy bread from Makkah and Jeddah: a fermented pouring batter is cooked on a griddle until full of holes, then the rounds are stacked, brushed with ghee and sprinkled with sugar and cardamom, and served for breakfast or with tea. This version mixes whole wheat into the white flour and cuts the ghee and sugar by more than half.
ingredients: 1½ tsp instant yeast (5 g) and a pinch of salt (0.5 g)
1 tsp olive oil (5 g) to wipe the pan
4 tsp sugar (16 g) mixed with 1 tsp ground cardamom
steps: In a blender mix the egg, warm water and yeast for 1 minute, then add both flours, milk powder and salt gradually while blending to a smooth batter thinner than cake batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until bubbles appear on top.
Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a paper towel dipped in a little oil.
Stir the batter, pour a small ladle into the pan and swirl to cover the base thinly.
Cook until the top is full of holes and dry and the base is golden (1–2 minutes), then flip for a few seconds if you like. Repeat to make about 12 rounds.
Stack the rounds on a plate, brushing each with a thin layer of ghee and sprinkling with a little of the sugar and cardamom.
Serve warm with tea or a glass of low-fat laban.
hints: What changed: 12 g ghee instead of 80 g butter, 16 g sugar instead of 3 tbsp or a heavy dusting of icing sugar, about 40% of the flour is whole wheat, the milk powder is nonfat, and the pan is only wiped with oil.
Kidney tip: milk powder and brown flour add phosphorus and potassium; you can use only white flour and leave out the milk powder, and keep to three rounds.
Diabetes tip: one serving has about 44 g carbohydrate; you can skip the sugar on top and keep just the cardamom, and eat it with an egg or low-fat cheese to slow the rise in blood sugar.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Mawdoo3, Al Jawhara Magazine

title: Madina Dagga (Spice Blend)
description: Madina dagga is a spice blend from Al-Madinah of toasted coriander seed, cumin and black pepper with sesame, citric acid and dried Madina roses, sprinkled on yoghurt, eggs and salad and served at Ramadan iftar spreads. This is a small home batch with far less salt than usual and a higher share of sesame and spices.
ingredients: 1 tbsp dried Madina rose petals (5 g), optional
steps: Toast the coriander seeds in a dry pan over low heat for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until they darken slightly and smell fragrant, then tip onto a plate.
Toast the cumin in the same pan for just 2–3 minutes until fragrant, then the sesame until golden, and let everything cool.
Grind the coriander, cumin, black pepper, dried rose, citric acid and salt to a fine powder in a spice grinder.
Stir the whole toasted sesame into the powder and mix well.
Keep the dagga in a sealed jar in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months; serve 1 tbsp over low-fat yoghurt, eggs or salad.
hints: What changed: 3 g salt for the whole batch (about 1.4%) instead of table salt plus kamrani salt at around 5% in the traditional blend; the sour citric acid and toasted spices make up for the salt.
Kidney tip: sesame and cumin contain phosphorus and potassium; one tablespoon is fine, but watch what you serve it with: yoghurt is a source of phosphorus, so keep it to half a pot.
Diabetes tip: the dagga itself is low in carbohydrate (about 4 g per tablespoon); serve it with eggs, vegetables and salad for strong flavour without sugar.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Tawabel7 spice shop

title: Pigeon Kabsa
description: Najdi pigeon kabsa cooks pigeons with onion, tomato and spices, browns them in the oven and cooks the rice in their broth with black lime. This version removes the pigeon skin and uses one tablespoon of oil, a broth with no stock cubes and little salt.
serving_size: 1 plate (1 pigeon with about 150 g rice)
ingredients: 4 small pigeons (about 1.2 kg whole), cleaned and skinned (about 480 g meat)
3 pierced dried black limes, 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods
1½ tsp salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), 1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp turmeric
steps: Wash the rice, soak it for 30 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic and tomatoes and cook 5 minutes until thick.
Add the pigeons and turn them in the mixture until they change colour, then add the cinnamon, cardamom, cumin, kabsa spice, chilies and salt and stir for 5 minutes.
Pour in the hot water, cover and simmer 30–40 minutes until the pigeons are tender.
Lift the pigeons onto a tray, brush with the lemon juice and a pinch of turmeric and brown them in an oven preheated to 220 °C for 10–15 minutes.
Skim the fat off the broth, keep about 375 ml in the pot, add the rice and loomi and boil on high heat until the broth drops.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes.
Spread the rice on a platter, place the pigeons on top and serve with green salad.
hints: What changed: the pigeon skin and most of its fat are removed, one tablespoon of oil replaces the usual generous amount, the pigeons are browned in the oven instead of fried, and no stock cubes are used.
Kidney tip: pigeon meat is high in phosphorus and protein and tomatoes add potassium; one small pigeon per person is enough, and do not drink the extra broth.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 50 g carbohydrate; serve with a large salad, and you can mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Cookpad, Cookinsta

title: Jazani Maghash
description: Maghash is a traditional dish from the Jazan region, slow-cooked in a stone pot (the maghash) inside the mifa oven or a home oven: lamb with okra, potato, tomato, onion and spices. This version uses lean lamb, one spoon of oil, more vegetables, no stock cubes and little salt.
ingredients: 560 g lean boneless lamb, trimmed and cubed
1 medium potato, cut and soaked (150 g)
1 green bell pepper (100 g) and 1 hot chilli (15 g)
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp black pepper, ¼ tsp cardamom
steps: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Brush a stone maghash pot, or a heavy ovenproof pot or clay casserole, with the oil.
Crush the garlic with the cumin, coriander, black pepper, cardamom and salt, and rub the mixture into the meat.
Drain the potato. Layer the onion in the pot, then the okra and meat, then the tomato, potato, zucchini and peppers.
Add the hot water and cover tightly with a lid or foil.
Cook in the oven for 2 hours until the meat is very tender; check after an hour and add a little water if it looks dry.
Serve it bubbling in the same pot.
hints: What changed: lean meat, one spoon of oil for the whole pot, no stock cubes, less than ¼ tsp salt per portion, and more vegetables.

Kidney tip: the tomato, potato and okra contain potassium and the meat contains phosphorus; boil the cut potato or soak it in hot water for 2 hours and discard the water, or replace it with more zucchini, and keep to one portion.

Diabetes tip: one portion has only about 20 g carbohydrate; it is traditionally served with rice or bread, so keep to 150 g cooked rice (basmati or brown) or half a whole-wheat flatbread with a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Yummy Layalina, Cookinsta, Saudi Press Agency

title: Hijazi Habb Soup
description: Habb soup is one of the best-known Ramadan soups of Makkah and Jeddah: whole white wheat grains simmered for a long time with a bag of whole spices, then cooked with meat and fresh tomato juice. This version uses lean meat, no stock cubes, less salt and ghee, and the fibre-rich whole grain.
ingredients: 170 g whole white wheat grains (habb), washed and soaked 6 hours
450 g lean lamb leg, trimmed of fat, cut in small pieces
400 g tomatoes, blended to fresh juice
Spice bag: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 piece galangal, 1 dried lime (loomi), 1 bay leaf, a little sheeba (lichen spice)
½ tsp cumin and ½ tsp black pepper
1 small handful fresh coriander, chopped (10 g)
steps: Put the drained wheat in a pot with 2 l water and the spice bag, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook for 2 hours, adding water whenever it runs low.
In a pan, soften the onion in the ghee, then add the meat and stir until it changes colour.
When the wheat is soft and split, pulse it briefly with a hand blender to thicken, then add the meat and onion, tomato juice and paste.
Add the cumin, pepper and salt and simmer for another hour, stirring now and then so it does not stick, until the meat is tender.
Remove the spice bag, adjust the thickness with a little hot water, sprinkle with coriander and serve hot.
hints: What changed: lean meat instead of fatty meat on the bone, no stock cubes, a little ghee and less than half the usual salt; the white version is made the same way with low-fat milk instead of tomato.
Kidney tip: whole wheat and meat contain phosphorus and the tomato adds potassium; keep to one bowl, and you can halve the tomato.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 27 g carbohydrate with 5 g fibre; if you have the soup, cut down on rice or bread in the same meal.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Al Bayan, WebTeb

title: Hijazi Ma'doos (Rice and Lentils)
description: Ma'doos is rice and red lentils cooked with onion, cumin and turmeric to a thick porridge-like texture, a winter favourite in Makkah, Jeddah and Madinah served with a dill yoghurt salad. We used more lentils than rice, browned the topping onions in a little oil instead of deep-frying them, and cut the ghee and salt.
ingredients: 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
1 small onion, thinly sliced (100 g), with 1 tsp olive oil (4.5 g)
1 cucumber, finely diced (100 g), and a handful of chopped dill (10 g)
steps: Wash the lentils and rice well, soak them in hot water for 30 minutes and drain.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion over medium heat until soft and starting to colour, then add the garlic for 1 minute.
Add the lentils, rice, cumin, turmeric and pepper and stir for 2 minutes, then pour in 1.2 l of the hot water.
Bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook for 35–40 minutes, stirring every few minutes and adding the remaining water as needed, until thick and smooth.
Add the salt in the last 5 minutes of cooking.
For the topping: toss the sliced onion with the teaspoon of oil and bake at 200 °C for 15–20 minutes until browned, or brown it in a non-stick pan.
For the salad: mix the yoghurt with the cucumber, dill and pinch of salt.
Ladle out the ma'doos, drizzle with the melted ghee, top with the browned onions and serve with the yoghurt salad, radishes and leafy greens.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, more lentils than rice, oven-browned instead of deep-fried onions, 1 tsp ghee for the whole pot, and less than half the usual salt.
Kidney tip: lentils and yoghurt are high in potassium and phosphorus; soak and rinse the lentils well, use equal amounts of rice and lentils, and keep the yoghurt salad to 2 tbsp.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 57 g carbohydrate but plenty of fibre and protein from the lentils; serve it with grilled fish and a large salad rather than a bigger portion.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Cookpad, Yummy (Layalina)

title: Southern Bread with Broth
description: A traditional meal from southern Saudi Arabia (Asir and Al-Baha): whole-wheat bread from the tannour or oven, dipped into a meat broth (marag) and vegetable stew (idam). This version uses lean lamb, more vegetables, no stock cubes, little salt and a whole-wheat bread.
serving_size: 1 small bread with a bowl of broth and stew (450 g)
ingredients: 180 g whole-wheat (burr) flour and 60 g white flour
2 tsp sesame and nigella seeds (5 g)
520 g lean boneless lamb, trimmed and cut into small cubes
1 large onion, chopped (150 g) and 2 garlic cloves (10 g)
2 tomatoes, grated (200 g) and 1 tbsp no-salt tomato paste (15 g)
150 g green beans, 200 g zucchini and 150 g carrots, cut small
1 small potato, cut and soaked (120 g)
1 green bell pepper (80 g) and 1 hot chilli (15 g)
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), ½ tsp cumin, 1 cinnamon stick
steps: For the bread: mix both flours with the yeast and salt, add the warm water gradually and knead to a soft dough. Cover and leave to rise for 45–60 minutes.
For the marag: heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the meat and garlic and stir until the meat changes colour.
Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, spices and cinnamon and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the hot water and salt, cover and simmer for 50 minutes until the meat is almost tender.

Drain the potato, add it with the beans, carrots, zucchini and peppers, and cook for 20–25 minutes until the vegetables are tender. Ladle some clear broth into small bowls and keep the rest as a thicker idam.
While the marag cooks, heat the oven to 230 °C with a tray inside. Divide the dough into 4 pieces, flatten them with wet hands and sprinkle with the sesame and nigella seeds.
Bake the breads on the hot tray with bottom heat for 8–10 minutes, then switch to top heat until golden.
Serve each hot bread with a bowl of broth and idam.
hints: What changed: lean meat, no stock cubes, less than ¼ tsp salt per portion, one spoon of oil for the whole pot, more vegetables, and a whole-wheat bread instead of white bread with ghee and honey.

Kidney tip: the meat and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus, and the tomatoes, tomato paste and potato add potassium; soak the cut potato in hot water for 2 hours or boil it and discard the water, or leave out the potato and paste, and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 66 g carbohydrate, mostly from the bread; you can eat half the bread with more vegetables and a green salad.
Best kept as an occasional dish for kidney, diabetes and heart diets; keep to one serving.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, M3aarf

title: Mathriya
description: Mathriya is a traditional winter dish from southern Saudi Arabia: whole-wheat flour is rubbed with a little water into small crumbs, cooked in boiling water until thick, and served with ghee and honey. This version uses whole-wheat flour, little salt, and about half the usual ghee and honey.
ingredients: about 900 ml water (800 ml for boiling and 100 ml for rubbing)
steps: Bring 800 ml water with the salt to the boil in a pot over medium heat.
Spread the flour in a wide dish, sprinkle the remaining water over it a little at a time and rub it with your fingertips until it forms small crumbs like coarse sand.
Add the crumbs to the boiling water gradually, stirring all the time, until it reaches the thick texture you like.
Lower the heat and cook for 20–30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the raw flour taste is gone.
Spoon it into 4 small bowls, make a small hollow in the middle, add 3 g ghee and 1 tsp honey to each and serve hot.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour, very little salt (usual recipes use a whole tablespoon), and about half the usual ghee and honey.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour has more phosphorus and potassium than white flour; you can use half whole-wheat and half white flour, and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 42 g carbohydrate; you can skip the honey and sprinkle a little cinnamon, and have it with a boiled egg or low-fat laban to slow the rise in blood sugar.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Elbalad News, Just Food

title: Meat Madghoot
description: Madghoot is a Saudi kabsa made in a pressure cooker: lamb is cooked with onion, tomato, spices and black lime, then the rice goes into the broth and finishes in the same pot. This version uses lean lamb, less oil, soaked potato to lower potassium, and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 600 g lean boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut into medium pieces
2 tbsp tomato paste, no salt added (30 g)
2 pierced dried black limes, 2 cinnamon sticks, 4 cardamom pods
2 tsp salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp black pepper
steps: Soak the potato cubes in warm water for 2 hours (change the water once), then drain. Wash the rice, soak it for 30 minutes and drain.
Heat the oil in the pressure cooker and cook the onion with the loomi, cinnamon, cardamom, cumin and black pepper until soft.
Add the lamb and brown it lightly, then add the tomato paste, tomatoes, kabsa spice and garlic and stir for 3 minutes.
Pour in the hot water, close the pressure cooker and cook 30–35 minutes after it comes to pressure on medium heat.
Release the steam, open the pot, skim off the fat and add the salt. You need about 400 ml broth; top up with water or boil to reduce.
Add the potato, rice and chilies and boil uncovered until the broth drops, then close the lid and cook on very low heat for 12–14 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave the pot closed for 10 minutes before opening.
Spoon the madghoot onto a platter with the lamb on top and serve with a tomato, onion and cucumber salad.
hints: What changed: trimmed lamb leg with the fat skimmed from the broth, less than half the usual oil, no stock cubes, and limited salt.

Kidney tip: potato, tomatoes and tomato paste are high in potassium and the meat is high in phosphorus; soak the potato as in the first step or leave it out, and keep to the meat portion (about 100 g cooked).
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 58 g carbohydrate; serve with a large salad, and you can leave out the potato or mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Layalina, Meat and More

title: Lamb Marqooq
description: Marqooq is a Najdi winter dish, the official dish of the Riyadh region, in which thin sheets of whole-wheat dough are cooked in a meat and vegetable stew. This version uses lean meat, more vegetables and a little olive oil, with no stock cubes or ghee and less salt.
ingredients: a pinch of salt (1 g) and a pinch of turmeric
560 g lean lamb leg, cut in medium pieces
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 2 pierced dried limes (loomi)
2 zucchini, cut in large pieces (200 g)
1 small eggplant, cut in pieces (150 g)
1 whole red or green chilli (15 g)
1 small onion, finely chopped (50 g), mixed with ½ tsp ground dried lime
steps: Mix the flour, salt and turmeric, add the water gradually and knead to a firm dough slightly stiffer than pastry dough, then cover for 30 minutes, knead again and divide into 8 balls.
In a heavy pot heat the oil and cook the onion until soft, then add the tomato paste and tomatoes and stir for 2 minutes.

Add the meat, cumin and bezar and stir for 10 minutes, then pour in the boiling water, add the dried limes and simmer on medium heat for 45 minutes until the meat is almost tender (or 20 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Roll each ball on a floured surface into a very thin round about 25 cm across.
With the stew boiling, lay one sheet on the surface and cover the pot for 1 minute, then push it aside with a spoon and add the next sheet; repeat until all the dough is used.
Add the zucchini, eggplant, chilli and salt around the sides, cover and cook on low heat for 40 minutes, stirring gently from the bottom, and add hot water if it gets too thick.
Add the pumpkin for the last 15 minutes until tender, then serve the marqooq hot topped with the onion and dried lime.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes and no browned butter or ghee, lean meat, a little olive oil, more vegetables and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour, tomatoes, tomato paste, pumpkin and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one plate, you can swap half the whole-wheat flour for white flour, halve the tomatoes and drink only a little of the broth. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 59 g carbohydrate with 10 g fibre from the whole-wheat flour and vegetables; do not add bread or rice, and add a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Marqooq), Mawdoo3

title: Lamb and Vegetable Thareed
description: Thareed is an old Arabian dish found across Najd and the rest of Saudi Arabia: torn qursan or thin flatbread soaked in a spiced lamb and vegetable broth and topped with the meat and vegetables. This version uses lean lamb, homemade whole-wheat bread and more vegetables, with no stock cubes, little salt and less ghee.
ingredients: 600 g boneless lamb leg, trimmed of fat and cubed
1 small eggplant, cut in chunks (150 g)
2 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 1 tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper, 1 pierced dried lime (loomi)
200 g whole-wheat flour with a pinch of salt (1 g) and about 140 ml water
1 small onion, sliced (50 g), with 2 tsp ghee (9 g), ½ tsp ground dried lime and a pinch of turmeric
steps: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic and lamb and stir until browned.
Add the spices, dried lime, tomato paste and blended tomato and stir for 5 minutes.
Add 1.5 l water, cover and simmer for about 1 hour until the lamb is nearly tender, skimming off any fat.
Meanwhile knead the flour, salt and water into a soft dough, divide into 4 balls, roll thin and cook on a hot griddle for 1 minute per side.
Add the carrots and pumpkin to the stew; after 10 minutes add the zucchini, eggplant and chilli and cook 15–20 minutes until tender, then add the salt.
For the topping: cook the onion in the ghee over medium heat until golden, then add the ground dried lime and turmeric.
Tear the bread into a deep dish, soak it with broth layer by layer, then top with the lamb and vegetables and finish with the onion topping.
hints: What changed: boneless trimmed lamb, homemade whole-wheat bread instead of shop bread, more vegetables, no stock cubes, and only a little ghee for the onion topping.

Kidney tip: the broth, tomatoes, pumpkin and carrots are high in potassium, and meat and whole-wheat flour are high in phosphorus; take less broth, keep to about 100 g cooked meat, and you can boil the vegetables in separate water and drain them to cut potassium.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 54 g carbohydrate, mostly from the bread; eat the vegetables and meat first, and whole-wheat bread raises blood sugar more slowly than white bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Hasawi Mubassal Bread
description: Mubassal (also called mudabbas or marasee') is a traditional bread from Al-Ahsa in the Eastern Province: a soft batter of whole-wheat flour, spring onion and spices, cooked in rounds in a pan and drizzled with date syrup. Here the rounds are cooked in a non-stick pan with a brush of olive oil, with little salt and a measured amount of date syrup.
ingredients: 6 pitted dates (50 g), soaked in 100 ml hot water
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar) and ½ tsp ground cinnamon
a pinch of saffron soaked in 1 tbsp water
steps: Mash the soaked dates with a fork in their soaking water to a smooth paste.
In a large bowl mix the flour, spices, cinnamon, salt and sesame, then add the spring onion, onion, mashed dates, egg and saffron.
Add the water gradually while mixing to a thick, soft batter similar to luqaimat batter, then let it rest for 10 minutes.
Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and brush it lightly with oil.

Pour in a small ladle of batter and spread it with the back of the spoon into a round about 12 cm wide; cook for 2–3 minutes until browned underneath, then flip and brown the other side. Repeat with the rest of the batter to make 8 rounds, brushing the pan with oil between batches.
Cut the rounds as you like, drizzle with the date syrup and serve hot.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour, a brush of olive oil instead of plenty of oil, little salt and no salted seasoning mixes, and about half the usual date syrup.
Kidney tip: dates, date syrup and whole-wheat flour contain potassium and phosphorus; you can eat one round, swap half the flour for white flour and use less syrup.
Diabetes tip: one portion (2 rounds) has about 64 g carbohydrate; have one round with an egg or low-fat labneh and cucumber, and skip the syrup or use just 1 tsp.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Truffle (Faqa) Marqooq
description: Truffle marqooq is a seasonal Najdi dish made in winter and spring when faqa (desert truffles) are in season: whole-wheat dough sheets are cooked in a meat and tomato broth with the truffles and carrots. This version uses lean meat and a little olive oil, with no vegetable stock cubes and less salt.
ingredients: 540 g lean lamb leg, cut in small pieces
1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar)
3 tbsp chopped fresh coriander or parsley (15 g)
steps: Soak the truffles in warm water for 2 hours, then scrape the skin with a knife (do not peel them like potatoes), remove all sand and grit, rinse well and halve the large ones.
Knead the flour with the salt and water to a soft, smooth dough, cover for 30 minutes and divide into 8 balls.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and soften the onion and garlic with the cinnamon and cardamom, then add the meat and bezar and stir for 5 minutes.
Add the grated tomatoes and tomato paste and stir until thick, then pour in the boiling water and simmer for 40 minutes until the meat is almost tender.
Add the truffles and carrots and cook for 15 minutes until tender, then lift them out with a slotted spoon and set aside.
Roll the balls very thin to the size of a small flatbread and add them to the boiling broth one at a time, tearing each sheet with a fork as it goes in so the dough cooks light.
Add the zucchini and salt, cover and cook on medium-low heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring now and then so it does not stick.
Return the truffles and carrots to the pot with the coriander, leave for 5 minutes, then serve hot.
hints: What changed: no vegetable stock cubes, lean meat, little oil and about half the usual salt; the truffles give a rich flavour so the dish does not need more salt.

Kidney tip: truffles, whole-wheat flour, tomatoes, carrots and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one plate with only a little broth, and you can halve the tomatoes. The truffle values are estimated (calculated from white mushrooms). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 58 g carbohydrate with 10 g fibre; do not add bread or rice, and add a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Cookpad (marqooq with meat and faqa), Al Eqtisadiah newspaper

title: Sparkling Apple and Mint Drink
description: A cold, alcohol-free Saudi hospitality drink of apple juice mixed with sparkling water, slices of apple, orange and lemon and sprigs of mint, served in hotels and at gatherings since the 1970s. This version uses unsweetened apple juice for only a third of the jug and plain sparkling water instead of sweet fizzy drinks and flavoured malt drinks.
ingredients: 800 ml plain sparkling water (soda water), chilled
1 red or green apple (150 g), thinly sliced with the peel
1 orange (130 g), sliced with the peel
a small bunch of fresh mint sprigs (10 g)
steps: Put the apple, orange and lemon slices and the mint sprigs in a large jug and press the mint lightly with a spoon to release its aroma.
Add the apple juice, stir gently and chill the jug for 30 minutes so the flavours infuse.
Just before serving add the chilled sparkling water and ice and stir very gently so the bubbles stay.
Pour into glasses with some fruit slices and mint leaves and serve at once.
hints: What changed: unsweetened apple juice for only a third of the jug, and plain sparkling water instead of sweet fizzy drinks and sweetened flavoured malt drinks, so there is no added sugar in the glass.
Kidney tip: orange and apple juice contain potassium; for a low-potassium diet leave out the orange and use more apple and lemon slices, keep to one glass and count it in your daily fluid allowance.
Diabetes tip: one glass has about 14 g carbohydrate from fruit sugar; you can make the juice only a quarter of the jug and add more sparkling water.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Rauch Fruchtsäfte (story of the drink), Chocolates & Chai

title: Chicken Jareesh
description: Jareesh is one of the oldest Najdi dishes and a Saudi national dish: crushed wheat is cooked slowly with chicken or meat broth and laban until soft like porridge, and served with an onion topping (kushna). This version uses skinless chicken breast and laban made from low-fat yoghurt, with no stock cubes, cream or lamb fat, little oil and ghee and less salt.
ingredients: 200 g jareesh (crushed wheat), washed and soaked for 1 hour
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 2 bay leaves; plus 1 tsp cumin
300 g low-fat yoghurt whisked with 200 ml water (laban)
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 1 tsp ghee (5 g)
1 tbsp no-salt-added tomato paste (15 g), ½ tsp ground dried lime and a pinch of cinnamon
steps: Put the chicken in a large pot with the grated onion, whole spices and water, bring to the boil and cook on low heat for 25 minutes until done, skimming off the foam.
Lift out the chicken and shred it, and remove the whole spices from the broth.

Drain the jareesh and add it to the broth with the cumin and chilli, bring to the boil, then turn the heat right down, cover and cook for 2 hours, stirring every 10 minutes so it does not stick (or 40 minutes in a pressure cooker), adding hot water if it dries out.
Add the shredded chicken, laban, salt and lemon juice, stir well and leave on low heat for 20–30 minutes.
Mash the jareesh with the back of a heavy ladle or a jareesh masher until smooth and thick.
For the kushna: heat the oil and ghee and cook the onion on medium heat until soft and lightly browned, then add the tomato paste, dried lime, cinnamon and a splash of water and stir for 2 minutes.
Spoon the jareesh into bowls, top with the kushna and serve hot.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, cream, milk powder or lamb fat, skinless chicken, laban made from low-fat yoghurt, only 1 tsp ghee in the kushna and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: whole wheat, laban and chicken are high in phosphorus and potassium; keep to one bowl, and you can halve the laban and replace it with water plus lemon juice. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 50 g carbohydrate with 7 g fibre from the whole wheat; do not add rice or bread, and serve it with a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Jareesh), The National News (jareesh as a national dish)

title: Chicken Madfoona
description: Chicken madfoona is a quick Saudi and Gulf dish in which chicken rubbed with turmeric and spices cooks over onion, potato, carrot and pepper in a pressure cooker, is covered with rice and smoked with charcoal. This version uses skinless chicken and little oil, with no stock cubes or food colouring and limited salt.
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, cut in large pieces
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), 1 tsp turmeric, ½ tsp cumin, ¼ tsp black pepper
1 large onion, cut in rings (150 g)
1 large green bell pepper, sliced (150 g)
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
1 small piece of charcoal and ½ tsp oil (2 g) for smoking (optional)
steps: Soak the potato slices in warm water for at least 1 hour, then drain (this lowers the potassium).
Rub the chicken with the turmeric, ground spices and tomato paste and leave for 20 minutes.
Brush the bottom of the pressure cooker with the olive oil and layer the onion, garlic, potato, carrot and bell pepper, then put the chicken on top without water.
Close the cooker and cook on low heat for 10–12 minutes after it whistles, then release the steam.
Meanwhile boil the rice in plenty of water with the cardamom, cloves, salt and the teaspoon of oil for 6 minutes until half cooked, then drain.
Spread the rice over the chicken, close the pot and leave on low heat for 15 minutes.
To smoke: put the lit charcoal in a small foil tray on the rice, drip the oil onto it and close the pot for 5 minutes. Remove the charcoal and turn the madfoona out onto a platter.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken, no stock cubes or colouring, less oil, and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: potato, tomato paste, carrot and chicken are high in potassium and phosphorus; soak the potato as in the first step or swap it for zucchini, and keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked chicken and 150 g cooked rice). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 60 g carbohydrate from the rice and potato; take less rice and more salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Cookinsta (chicken madfoona), Sayidaty Kitchen (madfoon lahm)

title: Hunaini
description: Hunaini is a winter sweet from Najd and Qassim made of minced wheat bread and dates, warmed with butter or ghee and cardamom. In this version a thin whole-wheat bread made with low-fat milk is cooked in a dry pan, the large amount of butter is replaced by a little ghee, and there is no added sugar.
ingredients: ½ tsp ground cardamom and ½ tsp cinnamon
a pinch of saffron and a pinch of black pepper
steps: Whisk the flour with the milk and baking powder to a smooth, pourable batter like pancake batter.
Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat, pour in half the batter and spread it thin; cook for 4–5 minutes per side until cooked and browned. Repeat with the rest.
If the dates are firm, soak them in a little hot water for 5 minutes and drain.
Cut up the bread and mince it with the dates, alternating pieces, in a meat grinder or food processor until evenly mixed.
Melt the ghee in a pan over low heat, add the hunaini mixture with the cardamom, cinnamon, saffron and pepper and stir for 5 minutes until hot and cohesive.
Serve warm in small bowls with Arabic coffee.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat bread made with low-fat milk and cooked without fat, a little ghee instead of sticks of butter, no added sugar, and a small portion.
Kidney tip: dates are rich in potassium, and milk and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus; you can use water instead of milk and have half a portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 51 g carbohydrate; have half a portion after a meal with protein and vegetables, and do not add honey or sugar.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, WebTeb

title: Okra with Yogurt (Mukhtoum)
description: Mukhtoum is a Hijazi dish from Makkah and Madinah: meat simmered with whole spices is cooked with okra in tomato sauce, then "sealed" with yogurt so the sauce turns thick and tangy. This version uses lean lamb and fat-free yogurt, the okra is not fried, and there are no stock cubes.
ingredients: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 bay leaf and 1 pierced dried lime (loomi)
500 g small okra, fresh or frozen
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander and ½ tsp black pepper
¼ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar) and a pinch of saffron
steps: Trim visible fat from the meat, put it in a pot with 1 litre of water and the whole spices, bring to the boil skimming the foam, then simmer about 1 hour until tender. Strain and keep about 400 ml of the stock.
Heat the oil and ghee in a pot and cook the onion over medium heat until golden, then add the garlic and chilli and stir for 1 minute.
Add the grated tomato, tomato paste, cumin, ground coriander, black pepper and salt and cook for 10 minutes until thick.
Add the okra, meat and 300 ml of the stock, cover and simmer for 20–25 minutes until the okra is tender, keeping the sauce fairly thick.
Whisk the yogurt with the cornstarch, spices, saffron and a little warm stock, then stir it gently into the pot and cook 5 minutes on very low heat without boiling hard.
Turn off the heat, add the fresh coriander and lemon juice and serve hot.
hints: What changed: lean, trimmed lamb, fat-free yogurt, okra cooked in the sauce instead of fried, and homemade stock instead of stock cubes, with less salt.

Kidney tip: okra and tomato are high in potassium, and yogurt and meat contain phosphorus; use 2 tomatoes instead of 3, boil the okra in water and discard the water before adding it, and keep to a small plate.
Diabetes tip: the stew itself is low in carbohydrate (about 26 g); serve it with 150 g cooked basmati or brown rice rather than rice with vermicelli.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Chef Hessa (Cookinsta), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Jareesh Soup with Chicken
description: Jareesh soup is one of the best-known Ramadan soups in Saudi Arabia, made from cracked wheat with chicken or meat, tomato, onion and cumin. This version uses skinless chicken breast, just one spoon of olive oil, extra carrot, no stock cubes and little salt.
ingredients: 120 g jareesh (cracked wheat), washed and soaked 1 hour
Spices: 1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 2 bay leaves
To serve: 4 lemon wedges (about 20 ml juice) and a small bunch fresh coriander (15 g)
steps: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the chicken and stir until it changes colour.
Add the garlic, tomato, carrot, spices and bay leaves and stir for 3 minutes.
Pour in the water, bring to the boil and simmer 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked, then lift the chicken out onto a plate.
Add the drained jareesh to the broth and simmer, covered, for 40 minutes, stirring now and then; then add the oats and salt and cook 10 minutes more until thick.
Return the chicken to the pot, loosen with a little boiling water if needed, and remove the bay leaves.
Serve hot with lemon and fresh coriander.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes or butter, skinless chicken, little salt and extra carrot for flavour and fibre.
Kidney tip: jareesh and oats are whole grains rich in phosphorus and potassium; keep to one bowl and you can reduce the tomato and carrot. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 34 g carbohydrate with good fibre; count it in place of bread or rice at the same meal.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Fatafeat

title: Mutabbaq with Meat and Leek
description: Mutabbaq is one of Saudi Arabia's best-known street foods, especially in Jeddah and the Hejaz: a paper-thin dough filled with minced meat, leek and egg, folded into a parcel and crisped on a griddle. Here the dough is half whole wheat, the meat is lean, and it is cooked on a non-stick griddle with a wipe of oil instead of plenty of oil, without ready samboosa sheets or cheese.
ingredients: 1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) for kneading and stretching
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar) and a pinch of black pepper
1 tsp olive oil for wiping the griddle (4.5 g)
1 lemon, cut in wedges (about 15 ml juice)
steps: Mix both flours with the salt and half the oil, add the water little by little and knead for 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough.
Divide the dough into 4 balls, coat them with the rest of the oil, cover and rest for at least 30 minutes.
Brown the minced beef with the onion in a non-stick pan without oil until cooked and dry, then add the cumin, spices and pepper and let it cool.
Mix the meat with the leek, spring onion, tomato and salt, and beat the eggs separately.
Stretch one dough ball on a smooth surface with lightly oiled hands until it is very thin and almost see-through.
Put a quarter of the filling in the centre, pour a quarter of the egg over it, then fold the sides over to make a closed square parcel.
Heat a non-stick griddle over medium heat, wipe it with a little oil and cook the parcel until golden underneath, then turn and cook the other side until the egg is set (about 4 minutes per side).
Repeat with the remaining dough, cut each mutabbaq into squares and serve hot with lemon.
hints: What changed: half the flour is whole wheat, the lean meat is browned without oil, the parcel is cooked with a wipe of oil instead of a lot of oil, and the ready samboosa sheets and cheese are left out to cut sodium.
Kidney tip: egg, meat and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus and tomato adds potassium; keep to one mutabbaq, and you can use egg whites for one of the eggs and use less tomato.
Diabetes tip: one mutabbaq has about 53 g carbohydrate; serve it with a large green salad rather than sweet drinks.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Layalina Yummy, Arabizi Translations

title: Sweet Musabeeb
description: Sweet musabeeb are Saudi whole-wheat rounds cooked on a griddle and served at breakfast or teatime with honey. This version uses whole-wheat flour, low-fat milk, yeast instead of baking powder, much less sugar, and one teaspoon of honey per serving instead of plenty of honey and ghee.
ingredients: 2 tsp oil (9 g): one for the batter, one to wipe the pan
A pinch of salt (1 g), ½ tsp ground cardamom, ½ tsp nigella seeds
steps: Blend the milk, egg and one teaspoon of oil, then add the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and cardamom and blend to a smooth batter like a thick crêpe batter.
Stir in the nigella seeds, cover and leave in a warm place for 30 minutes.
Heat a griddle or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with the oil on a paper towel.
Pour a small ladle of batter into a round, cook until bubbles appear, then flip until golden. Repeat to make 12 rounds, keeping them covered so they stay soft.
Serve 2 rounds per person with 1 tsp honey (5 g) and unsweetened tea or Arabic coffee.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour instead of white, half the sugar or less, low-fat milk, yeast instead of baking powder (less sodium and phosphorus), and a measured amount of honey with no ghee.
Kidney tip: milk and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus; keep to 2 rounds, and you can replace half the milk with water and half the flour with white flour. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one serving has about 27 g carbohydrate, about 6 g of it added sugar; you can skip the honey and serve with low-fat laban or an egg.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Al Ain News (musabeeb), Arabic Wikipedia (Marasee)

title: Kawari' (Sheep Trotters) with Chickpeas and Wheat
description: Kawari' (also karaeen or maqadim) are sheep trotters slow-cooked with onion, tomato and whole spices, a popular winter breakfast in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf; in some regions they are cooked with chickpeas and wheat. In this version the broth is chilled and the set fat lifted off, with one teaspoon of oil and little salt, and no stock cubes or salted curry mixes.
serving_size: 1 bowl (2 trotters with chickpeas and wheat, about 400 g)
ingredients: 8 cleaned sheep trotters (about 1.6 kg with bone, giving about 400 g cooked meat and skin)
60 g whole wheat grain (hab/harees), soaked overnight
240 g canned chickpeas, drained and well rinsed (1 can)
Whole spices: 2 pierced dried black limes, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 tsp coriander seeds, 4 cloves, 5 cardamom pods, 1 slice fresh ginger
1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
2 tbsp lemon juice (30 ml) and chopped parsley (10 g) to serve
steps: Singe the trotters over an open flame to remove any remaining hair, then rub with lemon and wash well.
Boil them in water for 5 minutes, then discard the water and rinse again.
Heat the oil in a large pot (or pressure cooker) and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic and tomato and stir 3 minutes.
Add the trotters, the whole and ground spices and the drained wheat, and cover with the water.
Bring to the boil, lower the heat and simmer covered for 2–2½ hours until the meat falls off the bone (or 45–60 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Strain the broth into a bowl and chill it for a few hours or overnight, then lift off and discard the layer of set fat.
Return the broth to the pot with the trotters and wheat, add the chickpeas and salt, and simmer gently for 15 minutes.
Serve 2 trotters per bowl with chickpeas, wheat and a little broth, sprinkled with lemon juice and parsley, with a rocket (jarjeer) salad.
hints: What changed: the broth is chilled and the set fat removed (the key step, as trotters are rich in saturated fat), only 1 tsp oil, no stock cubes or salted curry mix, and chickpeas and whole wheat are added for fibre instead of lots of bread.

Kidney tip: chickpeas and whole wheat add potassium and phosphorus and the concentrated broth is rich in protein; rinse the canned chickpeas well or use fewer, and keep the broth in the bowl to a little.

Diabetes and heart tip: one bowl has about 32 g carbohydrate from the chickpeas and wheat, so little extra bread is needed; for heart patients trotters are an occasional dish, not a daily breakfast, because of their cholesterol.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Asharq Al-Awsat, Khiyam

title: Chicken Musabbak with Vegetables
description: Chicken musabbak is a Saudi home dish in which chicken is cooked with onion, tomato and spices until the sauce thickens, then vegetables are added; it is eaten with rice or bread. It is made here on the stove, as in most sources, with skinless chicken and little oil, without soy sauce, ketchup, mayonnaise or stock cubes, and with more vegetables and fewer potatoes.
ingredients: 600 g skinless chicken (300 g thighs and 300 g breast), in medium pieces
4 tbsp low-fat yoghurt (60 g) and 1 tbsp lemon juice (15 g) for the marinade
1 large onion, chopped (150 g) and 3 garlic cloves, crushed (10 g)
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf
1 tsp curry powder, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp black pepper
2 tomatoes, grated (250 g) and 4 tsp no-salt-added tomato paste (20 g)
2 carrots, sliced (150 g) and 100 g green beans
2 small potatoes, peeled and cubed (250 g)
1 large zucchini (200 g) and 1 green bell pepper (100 g), cut up
steps: Coat the chicken with the yoghurt, lemon juice, half the curry powder and half the garlic, and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Soak the potato cubes in warm water for at least 2 hours, changing the water once, then drain.
Heat the olive oil in a pot and toast the whole spices for 1 minute, add the onion and cook until soft, then the rest of the garlic and the ground spices.
Add the chicken with its marinade and stir for 5 minutes, then add the tomatoes and tomato paste and cover for 10 minutes until the sauce thickens, adding a little water if needed.
Add the carrots, green beans, potatoes, 100 ml water and the salt, and cover for 15 minutes.
Add the zucchini and bell pepper and cook 10 more minutes until the vegetables are tender and the sauce is thick, then sprinkle with coriander and serve with rice or whole-wheat bread.
hints: What changed: no soy sauce, ketchup, mayonnaise or stock cubes; the marinade is low-fat yoghurt, lemon and no-salt-added tomato paste. You can also bake it covered in a tray at 200 °C for 1 hour, as in the first reference.
Kidney tip: potatoes, tomatoes, tomato paste and yoghurt are high in potassium or phosphorus; soak the potatoes as in the steps or replace them with cauliflower or cabbage, and use less tomato paste.
Diabetes tip: the dish itself is low in carbohydrate; add only about 100 g cooked rice or 1 small whole-wheat flatbread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad Saudi Arabia, Sayidaty

title: Chicken Madghoot
description: Madghoot is a quick Saudi home dish in which chicken and then rice are cooked in a pressure cooker with whole spices and tomato. This version uses skinless chicken, a little olive oil, more vegetables, no stock cubes and much less salt.
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, cut in large pieces
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves, 1 pierced dried lime (loomi)
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp cumin, ¼ tsp black pepper
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
About 400 ml liquid for the rice (chicken broth plus boiling water)
steps: Heat the oil in the pressure cooker over medium heat and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic and whole spices for 1 minute.
Add the grated tomato, tomato paste and ground spices and stir for 3 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Add the chicken and turn it in the sauce, then add the carrot, zucchini and chilli.
Pour in 300 ml boiling water, close the pressure cooker and cook for 10 minutes after it whistles, then release the steam and open it.
Measure the liquid in the pot to about 400 ml (top up with boiling water or boil it down), then add the drained rice and the salt; the liquid should sit about 1 cm above the rice.
Close the lid and cook on low heat for 7 minutes after the whistle, then turn off the heat and leave 10 minutes before opening.
Fluff the rice with a fork and serve with a cucumber and leafy salad.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, skinless chicken, less oil, roughly half the usual salt and more vegetables in the pot.

Kidney tip: tomatoes, tomato paste, carrots and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one portion (90–100 g cooked meat and about 150 g cooked rice) and you can halve the tomatoes. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 50 g carbohydrate; eat the salad first, and you can swap a quarter of the rice for brown rice soaked for an hour.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Tefal Middle East (chicken madghout)

title: Hasawi Meat Kabsa
description: Hasawi kabsa comes from Al-Ahsa in the Eastern Province; its hallmark is plenty of onion seasoned with black lime and turmeric and cooked in ghee, with tomato, fresh coriander and a caramelised-onion topping. We kept the ghee flavour at one teaspoon per person and used lean lamb, a broth with no stock cubes and less salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut into medium pieces
3 medium onions, chopped (330 g): two thirds for the pot, one third for the topping
2 medium tomatoes, peeled and diced (240 g)
2 tbsp tomato paste, no salt added (30 g)
1 tsp ground black lime (loomi), ½ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp ground cardamom, 1½ tsp salt-free mixed spice (bezar)
Whole spices: 2 pierced dried black limes, 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods
steps: Wash the rice, soak it for 30 minutes, then drain.
Mix two thirds of the onion with the ground loomi, turmeric and mixed spice.
Heat 3 tsp ghee in a pot, add the spiced onion and whole spices and cook until soft and lightly browned, then add the garlic.
Add the tomato paste and toast it for 1 minute, then the tomatoes, bell pepper and half the coriander, and cook 5 minutes until thick.

Add the lamb and turn it in the mixture for 5 minutes, then the hot water and ground cardamom; cover and simmer 1½ hours until tender (or 35 minutes in a pressure cooker). Skim off the fat and add the salt.
Lift out the lamb, keep about 375 ml broth in the pot, add the rice and boil on high heat until the broth drops.
For the topping: cook the remaining onion in 1 tsp ghee with a splash of water until golden, then spread it over the rice with the lamb.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 25 minutes, then serve sprinkled with the rest of the coriander, with green salad.
hints: What changed: ghee limited to one teaspoon per person instead of pouring it over the top, trimmed meat, no stock cubes, and much less salt, relying on black lime and coriander for flavour.

Kidney tip: tomatoes and tomato paste raise potassium and the meat is high in phosphorus; on a low-potassium diet cut the paste to 1 tbsp and keep to the meat portion (about 100 g cooked). Skip a large yoghurt salad on the side if your phosphorus is high.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 54 g carbohydrate; serve with a large green salad, and you can mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Chef Hessa (Cookinsta), Food2mins

title: Meat Majbous
description: Majbous is a Gulf dish also cooked in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province: meat is cooked with onion, tomato, dried lime (loomi) and spices, the rice is cooked in its broth and the meat is served on top. This version uses lean meat, a little ghee with olive oil instead of a large amount of ghee, no stock cubes and limited salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean lamb in medium pieces (boneless weight)
Whole spices: 2 pierced dried limes (loomi), 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp black pepper
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
A pinch of saffron soaked in 2 tbsp rose water or water
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic and meat and stir until the meat changes colour.
Add the ground and whole spices, the tomato and the chilli and stir for 5 minutes.
Pour in the boiling water and simmer for about 1¼ hours until the meat is tender, skimming the foam and fat from the surface.
Lift out the meat and leave about 450 ml broth in the pot, then add the salt and the drained rice.
Boil the rice until it absorbs most of the broth, then sprinkle with the saffron, return the meat on top, cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes.
Warm the ghee in a small pan and toss the raisins for 1 minute, then scatter them with the almonds over the rice and meat; serve with salad and vegetables.
hints: What changed: 2 tsp ghee plus 1 tbsp olive oil instead of a large amount of ghee, trimmed meat with the fat skimmed off the broth, no stock cubes, and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: tomato, raisins, almonds and meat are high in potassium or phosphorus; you can leave out the raisins and almonds, and keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked meat and 150 g cooked rice). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 55 g carbohydrate; start with the salad, and you can replace a quarter of the rice with soaked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (majbous lahm), Mawdoo3 (majbous lahm)

title: Najdi Kishna
description: Kishna is a Najdi sauce of slowly browned onion with tomato, spices and dried lime, spooned over maraheef, masabib, jareesh and hareis or served beside rice. This version uses a little olive oil, no-salt-added tomato paste and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 2 large onions, thinly sliced or finely diced (300 g)
4 medium tomatoes, seeded and diced (400 g)
1 tsp ground dried lime (loomi), ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp cinnamon, ¼ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp paprika
steps: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat, add the onion and cook for 12–15 minutes until caramelised and deep golden; add a spoon of water if it starts to stick.
Add the garlic and spices and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and tomato paste, stir and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes until thick.
Add the salt and spring onion, stir for 30 seconds, then take off the heat and serve hot over maraheef or jareesh, or beside rice.
hints: What changed: a little olive oil instead of a finjan (about 60 ml) of oil or ghee, no-salt-added tomato paste, no stock cubes, and flavour from dried lime and spices instead of salt.
Kidney tip: tomatoes and tomato paste are high in potassium; use only 2 tomatoes with more onion, and keep to 2 tablespoons of kishna.

Diabetes tip: kishna is low in carbohydrate (about 13 g per portion) and adds flavour without needing more rice or bread. In the Gulf another version with raisins is called hashwa; raisins raise sugar and potassium, so use no more than a teaspoon if you add them.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Qassimy Kitchen (onion and tomato kishna), Sayidaty Kitchen (tomato kishna)

title: Hijazi Dibyaza
description: Dibyaza is a Makkah (Hijazi) sweet served at breakfast on the morning of Eid al-Fitr: apricot paste (qamar al-din) is cooked with cardamom, cinnamon and cloves until thick like jam, then soaked dried fruit and nuts are added. This version adds no sugar beyond the sweetness of the apricot paste and fruit, uses 2½ tsp ghee for the whole pot (about 1 g per portion) and a moderate amount of nuts.
ingredients: 200 g qamar al-din (apricot paste), cut into small pieces
700 ml hot water to soak the qamar al-din
steps: Soak the qamar al-din in the hot water for at least 1 hour until soft, and soak the apricots, figs and raisins in more hot water for 30 minutes, then drain them.
Soak the almonds and pistachios in boiling water for 10 minutes and slip off the skins; toast the pine nuts in a dry pan until golden.
Mash the qamar al-din with its soaking water with a spoon or blender until smooth and liquid.
Melt the ghee in a pot, add the cardamom, cinnamon and cloves and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the qamar al-din mixture, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and cook for 15–20 minutes, stirring, until it thickens a little.
Add the apricots, figs, raisins and dates and cook gently for another 10–15 minutes, stirring, until thick like a soft jam.
Turn off the heat, stir in the almonds, pistachios and pine nuts and remove the cinnamon sticks.
Serve warm or cold in small dishes; it keeps in a sealed box in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.
hints: What changed: no sugar added beyond the qamar al-din (the traditional recipe uses about 3 glasses of sugar), 12 g ghee instead of 2 glasses, a moderate amount of nuts, and a small portion.
Kidney tip: dried fruit (apricots, figs, dates, raisins) and nuts are very high in potassium; keep to 2 tablespoons on the day, and avoid it if you are on a low-potassium diet.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 30 g carbohydrate, mostly fruit sugar; have half a portion with an egg or low-fat cheese at the Eid breakfast rather than on its own.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Dibyaza), English Wikipedia (Saudi Arabian cuisine)

title: Muhalla (Date Sweet)
description: Muhalla, or date aseeda, is a Najdi winter sweet in which melted khalas dates are slowly cooked with whole-wheat flour, then served with ghee and black pepper alongside Arabic coffee. This version uses a higher share of flour and fewer dates, swaps the large amount of butter for a little ghee, and keeps the portion small.
steps: Soak the dates in 500 ml of boiling water for 10 minutes, then blend them with the rest of the water until smooth and liquid.
Pour the date mixture into a heavy pot and add the flour gradually while whisking so no lumps form, then add the salt and half the pepper and cinnamon.
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 15–20 minutes until it boils and thickens.
Add half the ghee, cover and leave on very low heat for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring every 10–15 minutes, until thick, glossy and dark.
Spoon the muhalla into a serving dish; melt the remaining ghee with the black lime and the rest of the pepper and cinnamon, pour it over the top and serve warm.
hints: What changed: fewer dates and a higher share of whole-wheat flour, no added sugar, much less fat than the usual butter, and a small portion.
Kidney tip: dates are rich in potassium; keep to half a portion (60 g) if your potassium is restricted, and ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 46 g carbohydrate from date sugar; count it as part of your meal, not an extra, and preferably have half a portion after a meal with protein and vegetables.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Qassimy.com, Al Bilad newspaper

title: Bulool Al-Makhamir
description: Makhamir are small pieces of risen dough from Najd that are dipped in bulool, a warm syrup of water, cinnamon, dried lime (loomi) and sugar with a little ghee. Here the makhamir are baked instead of fried, half the flour is whole wheat, the bulool sugar is cut by more than half and the butter is swapped for a little ghee.
ingredients: 2 tsp olive oil (10 ml) for the dough + 1 tsp (5 ml) for the tray
steps: Mix both flours, the milk powder, yeast, sugar, baking powder and salt in a bowl.
Add the egg and the dough oil, then the warm water little by little, and knead for 8 minutes to a soft dough that does not stick to your hands.
Cover the dough and leave it in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and oil a baking tray with the tray oil or line it with baking paper.
Roll the dough 1 cm thick and cut small 4 cm rounds (or roll small balls), set them on the tray and rest them for 10 minutes.
Bake the makhamir for 12–15 minutes until puffed and golden, using the top grill for the last 2 minutes if you like.
For the bulool: put the water on the heat, add the cinnamon, dried limes, sugar and salt and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the ghee and simmer the bulool gently for 15 minutes, then lift out the dried limes and pour the bulool into a deep dish.
Serve the warm makhamir next to the hot bulool so each piece can be dipped, or pour the bulool over them just before serving.
hints: What changed: the makhamir are baked, not fried; half the flour is whole wheat; the bulool uses 45 g sugar instead of about 150 g, 2 tsp ghee instead of 50 g butter, and a pinch of salt instead of 2 tsp.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and milk powder add some phosphorus; you can use all white flour and leave out the milk powder, and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 48 g carbohydrate; dip the makhamir lightly rather than soaking them, and have 3 pieces with unsweetened Arabic coffee.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sahha wa Hana, Mhtwyat

title: Jamriyya with Meat
description: Jamriyya is a whole-wheat bread baked on embers in the desert; in the Najdi and northern version it is crumbled, soaked with meat broth and topped with the meat, in the style of thareed. Here the bread is baked in the oven or in foil on embers, and the broth is made with lean meat, plenty of vegetables and no stock cubes, with only two teaspoons of ghee.
serving_size: 1 plate of soaked bread with meat and broth (about 450 g)
ingredients: 480 g lean boneless lamb (leg or shoulder), cut up, visible fat trimmed
1 large carrot, sliced (150 g) and 2 courgettes, sliced (200 g)
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, 1 dried black lime (loomi), pierced, 3 cardamom pods
steps: Mix the flour with the yeast and salt, add the warm water little by little and knead to a soft dough; cover and leave to rise for 1 hour.
Meanwhile heat the ghee in a pot, add the onion and stir until soft, then add the garlic and meat and stir until the meat changes colour.
