Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, spices, black lime and cardamom, then the water; cover and simmer gently for about 1¼ hours, skimming off the foam.
Add the carrot and courgettes for the last 25 minutes, then the salt at the end.

Heat the oven to 230 °C, press the dough by hand into a thick round on a sheet of foil lightly dusted with flour, and bake for 20–25 minutes, turning once, until cooked and browned. (Outdoors the round is set in foil on the embers and covered with a few hot coals.)
Let the jamriyya cool a little, then break it into small pieces in a pot or deep dish.
Pour the broth over the pieces a little at a time and press with the ladle until soaked, then move it to the serving dish, arrange the meat and vegetables in the centre and serve hot.
hints: What changed: lean meat with visible fat trimmed, little ghee (1 tsp per 2 portions), homemade broth with no stock cubes, more vegetables in the broth, and whole-wheat bread.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour, tomato and broth contain potassium and phosphorus; swap half the whole-wheat flour for white flour, pour less broth, and keep to 90–100 g cooked meat.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 63 g carbohydrate from whole-wheat bread; you can cut the bread to two-thirds of a portion and serve it with a large green salad.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad Saudi Arabia (jamriyya), Arabic Wikipedia (thareed)

title: Tannour Bread
description: Tannour bread (also called mifa or dooh bread) is a traditional bread from southern Saudi Arabia made mostly from whole-wheat flour with a little white flour and slapped onto the wall of a hot clay oven; it is served with broth, stews or haneeth. This is a home-oven version, mostly whole wheat, with little salt and no sugar or ghee.
ingredients: 1 tsp nigella or sesame seeds (3 g)
steps: Mix both flours with the yeast and salt, add the warm water gradually and knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and leave in a warm place for an hour until doubled.
Divide into 8 equal balls, rest for 15 minutes, then roll each into a long oval about half a centimetre thick.
Heat the oven to its highest setting (250 °C) with a baking stone or an upturned tray inside for 20 minutes.

Brush the breads with egg, sprinkle with the seeds, place them on the hot stone and bake for 6–8 minutes until puffed and golden. In a traditional tannour they are slapped onto the hot wall until cooked.
Wrap them in a clean cloth to keep them soft and serve hot.
hints: What changed: mostly whole-wheat flour instead of white, little salt, and no sugar or ghee in the dough; serve it with broth, stew or laban instead of ghee and honey.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour has more phosphorus and potassium than white flour; you can reverse the ratio (two thirds white flour) and keep to one bread with a meal.
Diabetes tip: one bread has about 33 g carbohydrate; let it replace rice in the meal, or eat half with a vegetable stew or broth.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, M3aarf

title: Hail Tamman
description: Tamman is a popular winter dish from the Hail region: short-grain tamman rice is slow-cooked with young camel (hashi) or lamb, tomato, pumpkin, zucchini and eggplant until it turns soft and creamy like jareesh. This version uses lean meat, more vegetables, and less oil, ghee and salt, with no stock cubes.
ingredients: 500 g lean boneless young camel (hashi) or lamb, fat trimmed, cubed
2 tomatoes, chopped (240 g) and 1 tbsp no-salt-added tomato paste (15 g)
1 tsp Hail spice mix (sarar) or bezar, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp ground dried lime
1 small onion, sliced (60 g), 1 tsp ghee (4.5 g) and a pinch of dried lime
steps: Heat the olive oil in a heavy pot and cook the chopped onion until soft and lightly golden.
Add the meat and stir for 5 minutes until browned, then add the spices and chillies and stir for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and tomato paste and stir until they break down, then add the pumpkin, zucchini and eggplant and cover for 5 minutes.
Pour in 1.5 l hot water and bring to the boil, then add the washed (unsoaked) rice and the salt and stir.
Cover and cook on very low heat for about 3 hours, stirring now and then and adding hot water as needed, until the rice and vegetables melt together into a thick, soft texture.
Fry the sliced onion in the ghee with the dried lime until golden, stir the tamman briefly, spoon it into a serving dish and top with the onion.
hints: What changed: lean, trimmed meat, more vegetables, only 1 tbsp olive oil and 1 tsp ghee, and no-salt-added tomato paste with no stock cubes.
Kidney tip: tomatoes, tomato paste, pumpkin, eggplant and meat contain potassium and phosphorus; you can use less tomato paste and pumpkin, add more zucchini, and keep to one serving.
Diabetes tip: short-grain rice cooked this long raises blood sugar quickly; keep to one serving and eat it with a green salad or low-fat laban.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Saraya News

title: Saj Bread
description: Rghfan (also called masabeeb) are small rounds made from a pourable batter of whole-wheat flour, water and yeast, cooked on a saj griddle; they are a speciality of Hail and Najd and are served with ghee, honey, date syrup or olive oil. This version uses whole-wheat flour, low-fat milk and little salt, and is served with a little olive oil instead of ghee and honey.
steps: Whisk the flour with the yeast, salt, milk and water by hand or with a mixer until you have a smooth, pourable batter slightly thicker than pancake batter.
Cover and leave to rise for about 30–45 minutes until bubbles appear on the surface.
Heat a saj or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a few drops of oil.
Pour a small ladle of batter into a medium round and leave it until holes appear on top and the base is cooked, then turn it and cook until lightly golden on both sides.
Repeat with the rest of the batter to make 12 rounds, brush them with the rest of the olive oil and serve warm.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour, low-fat milk instead of evaporated milk, little salt, and served with a little olive oil instead of ghee, honey and date syrup.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and milk contain phosphorus; you can replace the milk with water and use half whole-wheat and half white flour, and keep to 2 rounds.
Diabetes tip: 2 rounds have about 30 g carbohydrate; serve them with eggs or low-fat labneh and vegetables such as cucumber and tomato instead of honey or date syrup.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad, Qassimy

title: Hijazi Ashouriya
description: Ashouriya is a traditional Hijazi pudding of whole wheat grains and rice, slowly cooked, sweetened, scented with rose water and topped with nuts and dried fruit; homes in Madinah and Jeddah make it on the 10th of Muharram and share it with neighbours. This version uses less than half the usual sugar, skimmed milk and a moderate amount of nuts in small portions.
ingredients: 200 g whole wheat grains, soaked overnight
1 cinnamon stick, 6 cardamom pods and 3 cloves
2 tbsp rose water or kadi water
steps: Drain the soaked wheat and put it in a pot with the water, cinnamon, cardamom pods and cloves; cover and simmer for about 1½ hours until the grains are soft, adding hot water as needed.
Rinse the rice, add it to the wheat and cook 25–30 minutes until soft and thick, then take out the cinnamon, cloves and cardamom pods.
Dissolve the cornstarch in a little cold milk, add it with the rest of the milk, the sugar and ground cardamom, and stir constantly for 5–7 minutes until thick like a pudding.
Add the rose water and half the raisins and apricots, stir for 1 minute and take off the heat.
Spoon into 10 small bowls, top with the rest of the dried fruit and the chopped nuts, and serve warm or chilled.
hints: What changed: less than half the traditional sugar (80 g instead of about 200 g for the same amount of grain), skimmed instead of full-fat milk, and a moderate amount of nuts and dried fruit in small portions.
Kidney tip: whole wheat, milk, nuts, dried apricots and raisins contain phosphorus and potassium; keep to one small bowl and cut down the apricots and raisins or swap them for a little grated apple.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 37 g carbohydrate, including 8 g added sugar; eat it after a meal with protein and vegetables, and you can reduce the sugar further or use a sweetener.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Hia Magazine (Chef Fahad Bukhari), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Kubayba Hail
description: Kubayba Hail are grape leaves stuffed with rice and vegetables, folded into squares or hexagons and slow-cooked over lamb, onion and tomato; it is one of the best-known dishes of the Hail region. This version uses lean lamb, little olive oil, no stock cubes, less salt and more vegetables in the filling.
ingredients: For the bottom of the pot
600 g lean boneless lamb (shoulder or leg), cut in medium pieces, visible fat trimmed
For the bottom of the pot
For the bottom of the pot
For the bottom of the pot
5 garlic cloves (15 g) and 1 green chilli, slit (15 g)
250 g fresh tender grape leaves (or jarred leaves soaked in boiling water and rinsed well)
200 g Egyptian (short/medium-grain) rice, washed, soaked 30 minutes and drained
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½–1 tsp crushed hot red pepper (Hail sarar)
Juice of 2 lemons (60 ml) and about 700 ml boiling water
steps: Wash fresh grape leaves in cold water and drain; if using jarred leaves, soak them in boiling water for 10 minutes, then rinse well to remove the brine.
Mix all the filling ingredients (rice, onion, spring onion, tomato, parsley, tomato paste, oil, spices and half the salt).
Put a teaspoon of filling on the rough side of each leaf, fold in the sides and then the ends over them to make a small square or hexagonal parcel.
Lay the lamb in the bottom of the pot, then the onion and tomato slices, garlic and chilli, and pack the kubayba tightly on top.
Place an upside-down plate on the kubayba, mix the boiling water with the rest of the salt and a pinch of spices and turmeric, and pour it over the plate until it just covers the parcels.
Boil for 15 minutes over medium heat, then cover and cook on very low heat for about 2 hours until the meat and rice are tender, adding a little boiling water if it dries out.
Pour the lemon juice over, leave for 10 minutes, then turn the pot out onto a serving dish and serve with cucumber salad and low-fat laban.
hints: What changed: lean lamb instead of fatty meat, a little olive oil instead of a finjan (about 60 ml) of oil plus ghee, no stock cubes, much less salt and more vegetables in the filling.

Kidney tip: tomatoes, tomato paste, parsley and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus, and jarred grape leaves are high in sodium; use fresh leaves or soak jarred ones well, and keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked meat).
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 63 g carbohydrate from the rice and grape leaves; start with the salad, and you can replace a quarter of the rice with brown rice or coarse bulgur.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (Kubayba Hail), Saudipedia (Kubayba Hail ingredients)

title: Hijazi Yaghmish
description: Yaghmish is a baked Hijazi pastry filled with minced meat, onion and tomato, popular in Makkah and Jeddah during Ramadan. In this version half the flour is whole wheat, the meat is lean, and the oil and salt are much lower than in the traditional recipe.
ingredients: 1 medium egg (50 g): two thirds for the dough, the rest for glazing
1 tomato, peeled and finely diced (120 g)
A handful of chopped parsley (15 g)
½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar)
steps: Mix both flours with the salt, then add the yoghurt, oil and two thirds of the beaten egg, and knead while adding the warm water little by little until you have a soft, smooth dough.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, cover and leave to rest for 30 minutes.
Cook the minced beef in a non-stick pan without oil over medium heat until it changes colour and its liquid evaporates, then add the onion, spices and salt and cook for 5 minutes.
Take the filling off the heat and let it cool, then stir in the tomato, chilli and parsley.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a tray with baking paper.
Roll each ball into a thin circle about 15 cm across, put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the middle, fold in two opposite sides and then the ends to make a closed square parcel.
Place the parcels seam-side down on the tray and brush the tops with the rest of the egg.
Bake for 20–25 minutes until golden on top and underneath, and serve warm with a green salad.
hints: What changed: half whole-wheat flour, lean mince instead of fatty meat, a little olive oil instead of vegetable shortening, about a third of the usual salt, and oven-baked, never fried.
Kidney tip: meat, yoghurt and whole-wheat flour supply phosphorus and potassium; keep to 2–3 pieces, and use all white flour if your dietitian has asked you to limit phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one serving (3 pieces) has about 65 g carbohydrate; have 2 pieces with a large salad if it is part of the Ramadan iftar meal.
Best kept as an occasional dish for kidney, diabetes and heart diets; keep to one serving.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Yaghmish), Cookpad

title: Hijazi Buff
description: Buff is an old side dish from Medina, Makkah and Jeddah: a thin dough filled with minced meat, boiled egg and parsley, cut into squares and usually deep-fried, often served in Ramadan. Here the squares are baked with a light brush of olive oil, the dough is half whole-wheat with little salt, and the filling uses extra-lean meat.
ingredients: ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp ground cardamom, ½ tsp cumin
steps: Mix both flours with the salt and oil, add the water little by little and knead to a firm, slightly stiff dough; cover and rest for 1 hour.
Put the meat in a non-stick pan over medium heat and stir, breaking it up, until its juices evaporate; add the onion and stir for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the spices and salt and stir for 1 minute, then take off the heat, let it cool and mix in the parsley and chopped egg.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and line a tray with baking paper.
Divide the dough in two, roll the first half into a thin rectangle (about 30×20 cm) and spread the filling over it in a thin layer, then roll out the second half and lay it on top.
Cut into 12 squares, press the edges of each square with a fork to seal, place them on the tray and brush with the oil.
Bake for 20–25 minutes until puffed and golden, and serve hot with salad.
hints: What changed: baked instead of deep-fried, half whole-wheat flour, extra-lean minced meat, no custard powder or starch, and limited salt.
Kidney tip: meat and egg yolk contain phosphorus; you can use 1 whole egg plus 1 egg white, and keep to 2 pieces with a cucumber and lettuce salad.
Diabetes tip: one portion (3 pieces) has about 49 g carbohydrate; have 2 pieces with a large salad or vegetable soup.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Saudi cuisine: Madini buff), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Hijazi Fish Sayadiyeh
description: Sayadiyeh is a well-known coastal dish from Jeddah and Yanbu in the Hijaz: fish cooked in a broth flavoured with browned onions and whole spices, then rice cooked in the same broth so it turns brown. This version poaches the fish instead of frying it, browns the onions with little oil and splashes of water, skips stock cubes and keeps the rice portion moderate.
ingredients: 1 tomato, grated (150 g) and 1 tbsp no-salt tomato paste (15 g)
2 dried limes (loomi), pierced, 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf
1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
¾ tsp salt (5 g) for broth and rice together
steps: Season the fish with the lemon juice and half the cumin and pepper and set aside.
Brown the onions in the pot with the oil over medium heat for 20–25 minutes, adding a spoon of water whenever they stick, until deep brown but not burnt.
Blend the browned onions with the garlic, tomato and a little water until smooth, then return to the pot with the tomato paste, whole spices, turmeric and the rest of the cumin and pepper.
Add the water and half the salt, boil for 10 minutes, then add the fish and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes until just cooked.
Lift the fish onto a tray and put it, uncovered, in a 180 °C oven for 10 minutes before serving so the top colours a little.
Strain the broth, measure 450 ml back into the pot, add the drained rice and the rest of the salt, bring to the boil, then cover and cook on very low heat for 20 minutes until tender.
Spoon the brown rice onto a platter, set the fish on top and serve with green salad and lemon wedges.
hints: What changed: the fish is poached in the broth instead of fried, the onions are browned in just 4 tsp oil, there are no stock cubes, and the rice is 50 g raw per person.

Kidney tip: the fish and tomato raise potassium and phosphorus (about 1000 mg potassium per portion); swap the tomato for a little vinegar, and eat only 100 g fish if your doctor limits protein or potassium.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 53 g carbohydrate; you can make half the rice brown rice (it needs more water and time), and fill half the plate with salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookinsta, Mawdoo3

title: Hasawi Mufalaq with Shrimp
description: Mufalaq is a dish from Al-Ahsa in the Eastern Province: toasted jareesh (crushed wheat) cooked with shrimp, onion, tomato and spices until it soaks up the broth. This version uses a little olive oil instead of butter, fresh unsalted shrimp and little salt, without the fried onion and nut garnish.
ingredients: 400 g fresh shrimp, peeled and cleaned
Whole spices: 2 cinnamon sticks, 4 cardamom pods, 1 pierced dried lime (loomi)
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
To serve: chopped fresh coriander (15 g) and 1 tbsp lemon juice
steps: Toast the jareesh in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until golden, then rinse it, soak in boiling water for 1 hour and drain.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic, whole spices and chillies for 1 minute.
Add the shrimp and ground spices and stir for just 2 minutes, then lift the shrimp out and set aside so it stays tender.
Add the tomatoes and tomato paste to the pot and cook for 5 minutes until saucy.
Add the jareesh, boiling water and salt, cover and simmer for 35–40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the jareesh is tender and has absorbed the water.
Return the shrimp to the pot for 5 minutes on low heat, then serve topped with coriander and a squeeze of lemon.
hints: What changed: a little olive oil instead of butter, fresh shrimp instead of salt-treated frozen shrimp, little salt, and no fried onion or nuts.

Kidney tip: jareesh and shrimp are high in phosphorus, and tomatoes in potassium; keep to one plate and you can halve the tomatoes. Frozen shrimp often has added phosphate and sodium, so read the label.

Diabetes and heart tip: one plate has about 43 g carbohydrate from fibre-rich whole grain; serve with a green salad. Shrimp is low in fat but high in cholesterol (about 160 mg per plate), so do not add more.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Supermama, 7elwa

title: Mixed Vegetable Idam
description: In Saudi cooking an idam is a thick tomato-and-spice vegetable stew eaten with white rice; this one mixes potatoes, eggplant, zucchini, carrots and green beans. This version uses fewer potatoes and more other vegetables, a little olive oil and less salt, and does not fry the vegetables.
ingredients: 2 small potatoes, peeled and cubed (250 g)
1 large zucchini (200 g) and 1 carrot (100 g), cut up
1 medium onion, chopped (110 g) and 3 garlic cloves, crushed (10 g)
2 tomatoes, finely chopped (240 g) and 1 tbsp no-salt-added tomato paste (15 g)
½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp bezar, ¼ tsp black pepper, 1 pierced dried lime
steps: Soak the potato cubes in warm water for at least 2 hours, changing the water once, then drain.
Heat the olive oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic.
Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, spices and dried lime and stir for 5 minutes until thick.
Add the potatoes, carrot, green beans and eggplant, stir, then cover for 10 minutes on low heat.
Add the zucchini, bell pepper, hot water and salt, bring to the boil, then cook covered for 15–20 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened.
Remove the dried lime, sprinkle with coriander and serve hot with white or brown rice.
hints: What changed: fewer potatoes and more mixed vegetables, only 1 tbsp olive oil, no frying of the vegetables, and no-salt-added tomato paste with less salt.
Kidney tip: potatoes, tomatoes, tomato paste and eggplant are high in potassium; soak the potatoes as in the steps or swap them for cauliflower, use less tomato paste, and keep to one serving.
Diabetes tip: the idam itself is low in carbohydrate and high in fibre; serve it with about 100 g cooked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty, Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Aqit (Dried Laban Curd)
description: Aqit (also called baql, jameed or madeer) is Bedouin food from Najd and the north: sheep or goat laban is heated until it curdles, then strained, salted, shaped into small balls and dried in the sun, and eaten with dates and coffee or tea. Here it is made from low-fat laban with very little salt, because traditional aqit is very salty.
ingredients: 2 l low-fat laban (sheep, goat or cow)
steps: Leave the laban out of the fridge for a few hours if you like a sourer taste.
Put the laban in a pot over very low heat without boiling, stirring gently now and then, until it curdles and the yellow whey separates from the curd (30–45 minutes).

Strain the curd through muslin or a fine sieve and discard the whey, then return the curd to a clean pot over low heat, stirring constantly, until most of the liquid has evaporated and it no longer sticks.
Mix in the salt and let it cool until easy to shape.
Shape into small balls or discs the size of a walnut (about 20 pieces) and lay them on muslin or a clean towel to absorb moisture.
Cover with light muslin and leave in the sun or a dry, airy place for 1–2 days until firm and dry, then keep in an airtight box in the fridge.
hints: What changed: low-fat laban and very little salt (about 0.2 g per portion) instead of the large amount used for long storage, so keep it in the fridge and eat it within two weeks.
Kidney tip: aqit is rich in protein and phosphorus like other dairy foods; keep to 1–2 pieces a day and avoid salty shop-bought aqit.
Diabetes tip: aqit is very low in carbohydrate (about 2 g per portion); serve it with just one date or with cucumber rather than many dates.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Aqit), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Qassimi Kleeja with Dates
description: Kleeja is the best-known traditional sweet of the Qassim region: rounds of wheat dough scented with cardamom, cinnamon and ginger, filled with dates or date syrup and black lime, and baked. This version uses more whole wheat flour, a filling of dates alone, much less sugar, and less than half the usual ghee.
ingredients: 1 tsp baking powder (4 g) and a small pinch of salt (0.5 g)
1 tsp cardamom, ½ tsp cinnamon, ½ tsp ginger, ½ tsp ground fennel (habba helwa), a few saffron threads
½ tsp ground black lime, ½ tsp cinnamon, ½ tsp cardamom
2 tsp sesame seeds (6 g) or nigella seeds for the mould
steps: Mash the dates with the black lime, cinnamon and cardamom (warm them 2 minutes with a spoonful of water to soften), and divide into 20 small balls.
Mix both flours, sugar, baking powder, salt and spices, then rub in the ghee with your fingertips until evenly spread.
Add the milk gradually and knead to a soft, firm dough that does not stick to your hands, then cover and rest 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180 °C and line a tray with baking paper.
Divide the dough into 20 balls, flatten each in your palm, put a date ball in the middle and seal well.
Sprinkle the kleeja mould with a little sesame, press the ball into it to take the pattern, then turn it out onto the tray. (Without a mould: flatten into a thick disc and mark the top with a fork.)
Bake on the middle shelf for 15 minutes until golden underneath, then switch to top heat for 2–3 minutes to colour the tops.
Let them cool completely and store in an airtight tin.
hints: What changed: 2 tbsp sugar (25 g) instead of about 200 g, 40 g ghee instead of 200 g butter or tail fat, a date filling with no added sugar or syrup, and at least half the flour is whole wheat.
Kidney tip: dates, brown flour and baking powder (which contains phosphate) add potassium and phosphorus; keep to one piece, and you can use only white flour to lower phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one piece has about 19 g carbohydrate; have one piece with unsweetened Saudi coffee in place of dates, not alongside other sweets.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Saudipedia, Arab News

title: Mutazeez
description: Mutazeez is a Najdi winter dish popular in Qassim and Riyadh; it is like marqooq but the dough is stiffer and shaped into small, thicker discs that keep their shape in a meat and vegetable stew. This version uses lean meat, a little olive oil and more vegetables, with no ghee or sweetened spice mix and less salt.
ingredients: 1 tsp olive oil (5 g) and a pinch of salt (1 g)
560 g lean lamb leg, cut in medium pieces
2 tomatoes (200 g) with ½ green bell pepper (100 g), blended
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp turmeric, 2 pierced dried limes (loomi)
2 zucchini, cut in large pieces (200 g)
250 g pumpkin, cut in large cubes
2 whole red or green chillies (20 g)
1 small onion, finely chopped (50 g), with ½ tsp ground dried lime and a pinch of cinnamon
steps: Mix the flour, salt and oil, add the water gradually and knead to a slightly stiff dough, then cover for 30 minutes and knead again.
Shape the dough into walnut-size balls and roll each into a disc 6–7 cm across and 2–3 mm thick; dust with a little flour so they do not stick.
In a heavy pot heat the oil and cook the onion until golden, then add the garlic, tomato paste, bezar, cumin and turmeric and stir for 1 minute.
Add the blended tomato and pepper and the meat and stir for 10 minutes, then pour in the boiling water, add the dried limes and simmer for 40 minutes (or 20 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Add the salt, then drop in the dough discs in batches while the broth boils, stirring gently between batches.
Place the zucchini, pumpkin and chillies around the sides of the pot so the discs do not break, cover and cook for 15 minutes on high heat and then 45 minutes on low heat, adding hot water if needed.
Spoon the mutazeez into a serving dish and top with the onion, dried lime and cinnamon.
hints: What changed: no ghee or browned butter on top and no sweetened masmana spice or apricot paste, lean meat, little oil and about half the usual salt with more vegetables.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour, tomatoes, tomato paste, pumpkin and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one plate, you can swap half the whole-wheat flour for white flour, halve the tomatoes and drink only a little of the broth. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 60 g carbohydrate with 10 g fibre; the dough discs are the starch of the meal, so do not add bread or rice, and add a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Mutazeez), Atyab Tabkha

title: Cabbage Soup
description: Cabbage soup is a light home soup in the Saudi kitchen: cabbage cooked with dill, garlic, tomato, spring onions and pieces of chicken, finished slightly sour with vinegar. This version uses fresh chicken breast instead of salty smoked chicken, far less sugar and a limited amount of salt.
ingredients: 600 g green cabbage, cut in wide strips
1 small bunch spring onions, sliced (60 g)
1 tomato, grated (150 g) and 1 tbsp no-salt tomato paste (15 g)
1 tbsp flour (12 g) mixed with 100 ml water
¾ tsp salt (5 g) and ½ tsp black pepper
steps: Heat the oil in a pot and soften the onion and garlic for 2 minutes, then add the chicken and stir until it turns white.
Add the cabbage and water and bring to the boil until the cabbage wilts.
Add the tomato, paste, spring onions, dill, sugar, salt and pepper and simmer for 30 minutes.
Stir in the flour mixture and the vinegar and cook for 5 minutes until slightly thickened.
Serve hot; it should taste lightly sour.
hints: What changed: fresh chicken breast instead of salty smoked chicken, a pinch of sugar instead of a full spoon, and little oil.

Kidney tip: one bowl has about 700 mg potassium from the cabbage, tomato, dill and chicken; you can leave out the fresh tomato and dill to lower it, and cut the chicken to 40 g per portion if you need less protein.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has only about 18 g carbohydrate and plenty of fibre; serve it with a slice of wholemeal bread instead of white baguette.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, WebTeb, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Meat Madfoona
description: Madfoona is a Gulf home dish, rooted in the Yemeni pit-cooking tradition, in which spiced meat cooks over layers of onion, pepper and potato in a pressure cooker, is then buried under rice and turned out to serve. This version uses lean meat, little oil, a spoon of ghee instead of butter pieces, no stock cubes and limited salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean lamb, cut in medium pieces (boneless weight)
1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
1 large onion, cut in rings (150 g)
1 large green bell pepper, sliced (150 g)
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick
1 small piece of charcoal and ½ tsp oil (2 g) for smoking (optional)
steps: Soak the potato slices in warm water for at least 1 hour, then drain (this lowers the potassium).
Season the meat with the ground spices and tomato paste and leave for 20 minutes.
Brush the bottom of the pressure cooker with the olive oil and layer the onion, then the garlic, bell pepper, carrot and potato, and put the meat on top without adding water.
Close the cooker and cook on low heat for 30 minutes after it whistles until the meat is tender, then release the steam and open it.
Meanwhile boil the rice with the whole spices and salt in plenty of water for 6 minutes until half cooked, then drain.
Scatter the parsley over the meat, cover with the rice and dot the ghee on top, then close the cooker, bring to a whistle on high heat and cook 10 minutes on low heat.
To smoke: put the lit charcoal in a small foil tray on the rice, drip the oil onto it and close the pot for 5 minutes. Remove the charcoal, turn the pot out onto a platter and serve with salad.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, trimmed lean meat, 2 tsp ghee instead of butter pieces, carrot for more vegetables, and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: potato, tomato paste, carrot and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; soak the potato as in the first step or swap it for zucchini, and keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked meat and 150 g cooked rice). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: rice and potato together raise the carbohydrate (about 60 g per portion); take less rice when you eat the potato, and start with the salad.
Suitable for: a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (madfoon lahm), Yummy Layalina (madfoon lahm)

title: Qassimi Qishd
description: Qishd is a traditional Qassim sweet of toasted wholewheat flour cooked with dates and butter, served hot with Arabic coffee. This version uses much less butter, low-fat yoghurt instead of cream, no added sugar and small portions.
ingredients: 250 g pitted Sukkari or Khalas dates (about 20 dates)
½ tsp ground cardamom, ¼ tsp cinnamon, a pinch of ground ginger
steps: Toast the flour in a dry non-stick pan over low heat, stirring all the time, for 8–10 minutes until golden and fragrant.
Add the butter and stir it into the flour until melted and slightly crumbly.
Add the dates and stir and press with the spoon for 5 minutes until soft and mixed with the flour; add a little hot water if it gets dry.
Add the cardamom, cinnamon and ginger, then the yoghurt, and stir for 2 minutes over low heat until smooth.
Spread it in a serving dish, mark into 8 portions and serve hot with Arabic coffee.
hints: What changed: 25 g butter instead of 100–150 g, low-fat yoghurt instead of cream, no added sugar, and a small fixed portion (55 g) instead of a full bowl.
Kidney tip: dates are very high in potassium, and wholewheat flour and yoghurt contain phosphorus; keep to one small portion on special occasions and ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 30 g carbohydrate, mostly date sugar; eat it after a balanced meal rather than as a snack on its own, and do not have more than one portion.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (qishd), Atyab Tabkha (Qassimi qishd)

title: Jazani Potatoes with Sauces
description: Jazani potatoes are a popular snack from Jazan: thick potato fingers served with a spicy humar (tamarind) sauce and a garlic sauce. This version bakes the potatoes with one spoon of oil instead of deep frying, makes the garlic sauce with low-fat yoghurt, and uses little salt.
serving_size: 1 small plate with the sauces (230 g)
ingredients: ¼ tsp salt (1.5 g) and black pepper
40 g tamarind (humar) pulp soaked in 150 ml hot water
30 g green chillies and 15 g red chillies
3 garlic cloves (10 g) and 15 g fresh coriander
½ tsp cumin and 1 pinch salt (1 g)
1 garlic clove, crushed (5 g) and 2 tsp lemon juice (10 ml)
steps: Peel the potatoes, cut each in half lengthways, then cut each half into 3 thick fingers.
Boil the fingers for 5 minutes, drain and discard the water, and pat them very dry with a towel.
Heat the oven to 220 °C. Toss the potatoes with the oil and black pepper and spread them in one layer on a tray lined with baking paper.
Bake for 30–35 minutes, turning once, until golden and crisp (or air-fry at 200 °C for 18–20 minutes), then sprinkle with the salt.

For the humar sauce: strain the tamarind, keeping the liquid and pulp and discarding the seeds, then blend it with the paste, chillies, garlic, coriander, cumin and salt until smooth; thin with water to taste.
For the garlic sauce: whisk the yoghurt with the garlic, lemon juice and salt.
Arrange the potatoes on plates and drizzle with both sauces, or serve the sauces in small dishes on the side.
hints: What changed: potatoes baked with one spoon of oil instead of deep fried, a low-fat yoghurt garlic sauce instead of oil and starch or mayonnaise, and much less salt in the sauces (usual recipes add a spoon of salt to the humar sauce).

Kidney tip: potatoes, tamarind and tomato paste are high in potassium and yoghurt contains phosphorus; after cutting, soak the potatoes in hot water for 2 hours, then boil them in fresh water and discard it, so the real potassium is lower than calculated here, and use only a teaspoon of each sauce.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 38 g carbohydrate; serve it with a protein such as grilled chicken or fish and a green salad rather than as a meal on its own.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Elbalad News, Yummy Layalina

title: Musabeeb with Kashna
description: Musabeeb is a popular Najdi dish of rounds of pourable batter cooked on a griddle (saj), served savoury with kashna (stewed onion and tomato) or sweet. This version uses more whole-wheat than white flour, yeast instead of baking powder, very little sugar, and a kashna made with olive oil, more vegetables and little salt.
ingredients: A pinch of ground cardamom and of saffron
1 tsp oil to wipe the pan (5 g)
Spices: ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp ground dried lime, a pinch of cinnamon, turmeric and black pepper
Salt: ¾ tsp (4 g) in total: a pinch in the batter, the rest in the kashna
steps: Mix both flours with the yeast, sugar, cardamom, saffron and a pinch of salt, then add the egg and warm water gradually and whisk to a thick pourable batter like pancake batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 45 minutes until bubbly.

For the kashna: heat the oil and cook the onion until soft, add the garlic and spices for 1 minute, then the tomatoes, pepper and remaining salt, and cook 8–10 minutes until thick; turn off the heat and add the spring onions.
Heat a griddle or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it once with the oil on a paper towel.
Pour a small ladle of batter, spread it a little, and cook until bubbles appear and the underside is golden, then flip for 1 minute. Repeat to make 12 rounds.
Arrange the musabeeb on a plate, top with the hot kashna and serve with a green salad or cucumber.
hints: What changed: two-thirds whole-wheat flour, yeast instead of baking powder and milk powder (less sodium and phosphorus), only one teaspoon of sugar, and kashna made with olive oil instead of butter and ghee.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour is higher in phosphorus and potassium than white, and tomatoes are high in potassium; you can use half and half flour, use less tomato and more onion and pepper. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one portion (3 rounds) has about 44 g carbohydrate; the kashna and salad add fullness, and you can have a boiled egg instead of the third round.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Yummy Layalina (musabeeb with kashna), Sayidaty Kitchen (musabeeb with onion and sauce)

title: Oven Lamb Mandi
description: Meat mandi is a festive dish across Saudi Arabia and Yemen: lamb roasts slowly above spiced rice and is then smoked with charcoal. We use lean, trimmed leg of lamb, a low-fat yoghurt marinade and only a little ghee and salt.
ingredients: 560 g lean leg of lamb, visible fat trimmed, in large pieces
1 tsp mandi spice mix, ½ tsp turmeric, a pinch of saffron soaked in 1 tbsp water
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 30 minutes
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 2 tsp ghee (9 g)
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves, ¼ tsp black pepper
¾ tsp salt (4 g), split between meat and rice
1 small piece of charcoal for smoking (optional)
steps: Mix the yoghurt, spices, turmeric, saffron, garlic and ¼ tsp of the salt; coat the lamb and chill for at least 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 170°C. In a pot, soften the onion in the oil and ghee, then add the tomato and whole spices and stir 2 minutes.
Add the drained rice, the rest of the salt and the lukewarm water, and pour everything into a deep oven tray.
Seal the tray with two layers of foil and pierce holes, then arrange the lamb on top and cover it with more foil.
Cook for 2–2½ hours until the lamb is tender, then uncover the meat and brown it for 10 minutes on the top shelf.
Smoke the rice and lamb with a glowing piece of charcoal in a small metal bowl for 3–5 minutes under cover.
Serve the rice topped with the lamb and sprinkled with raisins, with a green salad.
hints: What changed: lean leg instead of fatty ribs, only 2 tsp ghee instead of a lot of butter, no stock cubes and much less salt.
Kidney tip: lamb, yoghurt and raisins add phosphorus and potassium; you can leave out the raisins and keep to 90–100 g cooked meat.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 50 g carbohydrate; for a lower-carb meal halve the rice and add roasted vegetables.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Mandi), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Hijazi Fool Mudammas
description: Fool mudammas is a famous Hijazi breakfast from Makkah and Jeddah: dried fava beans slow-cooked with a little red lentil and a date until soft, then served with tahini, cumin and dakous tomato salsa. This version uses less tahini and olive oil, little salt, and no ghee or stock cubes.
ingredients: 250 g small dried fava beans, soaked 12 hours
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) to serve
steps: Drain the soaked beans, cover with water by about 5 cm and cook over medium heat for 30 minutes (or 30 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Add the lentils and date and cook on very low heat for 1–2 hours (or 30 more minutes under pressure) until the beans are soft and the lentils have melted, adding boiling water if needed.
For the dakous: finely chop or briefly blend the tomato, garlic, coriander and chilli, then add the lemon juice.
Mash the beans lightly and stir in the salt, cumin, tahini and 3 tbsp of the dakous.
For a smoky flavour (optional): set a small bowl with a hot piece of charcoal in the middle of the beans, add a drop of oil, cover for 1 minute, then remove it.
Spoon into bowls, top with the remaining dakous, a pinch of cumin and the olive oil, and serve with whole-wheat bread.
hints: What changed: no ghee and no stock cubes, less tahini and oil, and less than half the salt of a typical fool shop.

Kidney tip: fava beans, lentils and tahini are very high in potassium and phosphorus; take half a bowl with bread and vegetables, and soaking the beans, changing the water several times and cooking them in fresh water lowers potassium a little.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 49 g carbohydrate and plenty of fibre (about 18 g); eat it with a small whole-wheat flatbread instead of tamees, with cucumber and tomato.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Mawdoo3

title: Fool Qallaba
description: Fool qallaba is a popular Saudi breakfast: cooked fava beans tossed in a pan with onion, tomato, green chilli and cumin until saucy. This version uses home-cooked unsalted beans and no stock cubes, with a little olive oil and a light drizzle of tahini.
ingredients: 200 g dried fava beans, soaked overnight and boiled without salt (about 500 g cooked)
1 tsp ground cumin, ½ tsp black pepper
To serve: 1 tbsp tahini (15 g) and 1 tbsp lemon juice
steps: Drain the cooked beans, keeping a little of the cooking water, and lightly mash half of them.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft and lightly golden, then add the garlic and chillies for 2 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, cumin and pepper and cook for 7 minutes until thick.
Add the beans, salt and a splash of the cooking water and toss over low heat for 5 minutes to absorb the flavours.
Spoon into a dish, drizzle with the tahini thinned with lemon, and serve with a rocket and cucumber salad.
hints: What changed: home-cooked unsalted beans instead of canned, no stock cubes, and only a little oil and tahini.

Kidney tip: fava beans, tahini and tomatoes are high in potassium and phosphorus; take half a portion and ask your dietitian about your amount. If you use canned beans, choose no-salt-added and rinse them well.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 39 g carbohydrate and about 15 g fibre; eat it with a small whole-wheat flatbread instead of white tamees.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Elwasfa

title: Truffle (Faqa) Madghoot
description: Rice cooked in a pressure cooker with faqa (desert truffles), tomato and green chilli, a Saudi home dish of the spring truffle season that lets the truffle flavour lead. Oil and salt are reduced and the dish stays as simple as the home version.
ingredients: 400 g fresh faqa (desert truffles), peeled, washed well and halved
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
steps: Soak the truffles in cold water, then scrub them with a brush and rinse several times until all the sand is gone.
Blend the tomatoes, chilli and black pepper until smooth.
Heat the oil in the pressure cooker, stir the truffles for 2 minutes, then pour in the tomato mixture and cook 3 minutes.
Add 300 ml hot water, close the cooker and cook 10 minutes after the whistle, then release the steam.
Add the drained rice and the salt and top up with water to about 400 ml of liquid, about 1 cm above the rice.
Close and cook on low heat for 7 minutes after the whistle, rest 10 minutes before opening and serve hot.
hints: What changed: a measured amount of olive oil instead of a lot of oil and much less salt, keeping the traditional simple style without onion or heavy spicing.
Kidney tip: truffles and tomatoes contain potassium; keep to one portion and you can use only 2 tomatoes. The dish has no meat, so it is lower in phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 47 g carbohydrate; serve with a green salad and a glass of low-fat laban to add protein.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arab News (Saudi truffle season), Tareekaa (truffle kabsa)

title: Hijazi Chicken Saleeq
description: Chicken saleeq is the home version of the famous Hijazi dish: rice cooked in chicken broth with cardamom and mastic, then beaten with milk until creamy, served with oven-browned chicken. This version uses skinless chicken, low-fat milk, little ghee and little salt with no stock cubes.
ingredients: 350 g skinless chicken breast and 250 g skinless chicken thighs (meat weight)
Whole spices: 5 cardamom pods, 1 bay leaf, 1 cinnamon stick, 2 mastic grains
200 g short-grain (Egyptian) rice, washed and soaked 1 hour
2 tsp ghee (9 g) with 2 mastic grains, to serve
2 tsp olive oil (9 g) with ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp mixed spices and black pepper, to brush the chicken
Salt: 1 scant tsp (5 g) for the whole pot
1 tomato (150 g), a handful of coriander (15 g), 1 green chilli (10 g), 1 tbsp lemon juice (15 ml), 1 small garlic clove (3 g), 60 ml cold water
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the water, bring to the boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and whole spices and simmer 30 minutes until the chicken is cooked, then lift it out and strain the broth.
Measure about 1 l of broth back into the pot, add the drained rice and half the salt and simmer 30–40 minutes until the rice is very soft; add a little boiling water if it dries.
Add the hot milk little by little and beat the rice with a wooden spoon until creamy and smooth, then leave 10 minutes on very low heat.
Brush the chicken with the oil, turmeric, spices and remaining salt and brown it under the oven grill at 220°C for 10 minutes.
Blend the dagoos ingredients and serve chilled.
Warm the ghee with the mastic for a few seconds, pour it over the saleeq in the serving dish, top with the chicken and serve at once with the dagoos and a green salad.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken browned under the grill instead of fried, low-fat milk instead of full-fat milk powder, very little ghee, no bouillon and much less salt.
Kidney tip: milk and chicken are high in phosphorus and tomato in potassium; keep to one portion (90–120 g cooked chicken), and you can swap half the milk for broth. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 51 g carbohydrate from soft, quickly absorbed rice; do not go beyond it, and start with the salad and dagoos.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Saleeq Taifi), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Red Meat Kabsa
description: Red meat kabsa is an everyday Najdi dish that takes its colour from tomatoes and tomato paste, with the rice cooked in the lamb broth with black lime and spices. This version uses lean, trimmed lamb leg, little oil, a homemade broth with no stock cubes and much less salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut into large pieces
1 small onion, sliced, for the topping (100 g)
2 tbsp tomato paste, no salt added (30 g)
3 dried black limes (loomi), pierced, and ½ tsp ground loomi
2 tsp salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp turmeric
Whole spices: 1 cinnamon stick, 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 2 bay leaves
steps: Wash the rice, soak it for at least 30 minutes, then drain.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pot, add the chopped onion, whole spices, whole loomi and chilies and cook until the onion is golden.
Add the lamb and brown it lightly on all sides.
Add the garlic, bell pepper, tomatoes, tomato paste and ground spices and stir for 5 minutes.
Pour in the hot water, cover and simmer for 1½ hours until the lamb is tender (or 35 minutes in a pressure cooker). Skim the fat from the surface, then add the salt.
Lift out the lamb and loomi, keep about 375 ml of broth in the pot, add the drained rice and boil on high heat until most of the broth is absorbed.
Return the lamb and loomi on top of the rice, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 25 minutes.
For the topping: heat 1 tsp oil in a non-stick pan and cook the sliced onion with a splash of water until soft and golden, then add the raisins and ground loomi for 1 minute.
Spread the rice on a platter, top with the lamb and the onion-raisin topping, and serve with green salad.
hints: What changed: trimmed lamb leg instead of fatty cuts, fat skimmed from the broth, far less oil, no stock cubes, and limited salt with more flavour from loomi and spices.

Kidney tip: tomatoes, tomato paste and raisins are high in potassium and the meat is high in phosphorus; you can cut the paste to 1 tbsp, skip the raisins and keep to the meat portion (about 100 g cooked).
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 60 g carbohydrate; serve with a large salad, and you can mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Munaty Cooking, Wikipedia (Kabsa)

title: Fish Majbous
description: Fish majbous is a coastal Gulf dish also cooked in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province: rice is cooked with onion, tomato, ginger and spices and topped with spiced fish such as kingfish (kanad). In this version the fish is pan-seared in a little oil instead of deep-fried, with no stock cubes and limited salt.
ingredients: ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp black pepper
3 garlic cloves, crushed (10 g), and 1 tbsp grated ginger (10 g)
½ bunch fresh coriander, chopped (20 g)
1 pierced dried lime (loomi), 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 4 cardamom pods, ½ tsp ground loomi
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
About 450 ml homemade unsalted fish stock (from the head and bones) or water
steps: Season the fish with the lemon juice, turmeric, cumin, coriander and black pepper and leave for 20 minutes.
Heat the fish oil in a non-stick pan and sear the fish for 3 minutes per side until golden but not fully cooked, then set aside.
Heat the second spoon of oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic, ginger and whole spices for 1 minute.
Add the tomato, chilli and half the coriander and stir for 5 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Add the stock and salt; when it boils add the drained rice and cook until it absorbs most of the liquid.
Lay the fish on the rice, cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes until the rice and fish are done.
Sprinkle with the rest of the coriander and serve with a green salad and lemon wedges.
hints: What changed: the fish is seared in one spoon of oil instead of being floured and deep-fried, homemade fish stock replaces stock cubes, and there is about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: fish and tomato are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one portion (about 110 g cooked fish and 150 g cooked rice), and you can halve the tomato. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 50 g carbohydrate; start with the salad, and you can replace a quarter of the rice with soaked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (Kuwaiti fish majbous), Khaleej Kitchen (fish majbous)

title: Chicken Hamsa
description: Chicken hamsa is a quick Saudi pan dish in which chicken pieces are tossed with onion, peppers, cabbage, carrot and spices, and eaten with bread or rice at home or on desert outings. This version uses skinless chicken breast and a little olive oil, no Maggi cube, and only 2 tsp of reduced-sodium soy sauce.
ingredients: 500 g skinless chicken breast, cut into small pieces
1 large onion, chopped (150 g) and 3 garlic cloves, chopped (10 g)
1 large green bell pepper, chopped (150 g)
1 tsp bezar, ½ tsp cumin, ¼ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp black pepper
2 tsp reduced-sodium soy sauce (10 g) and 1 tbsp lemon juice (15 g)
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over high heat, add the onion and chilli and stir until the onion softens.
Add the chicken and garlic and stir for 5–6 minutes until the chicken is white on all sides.
Add the bell pepper, cabbage and carrot and stir for 4–5 minutes until slightly soft but still crisp.
Add the spices and salt and stir, then add the parsley.
Add the soy sauce and lemon juice and stir for 3 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked; serve hot with whole-wheat bread.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken breast, only 1 tbsp olive oil, no Maggi cube, and a small amount of reduced-sodium soy sauce instead of sweet soy sauce.
Kidney tip: chicken supplies phosphorus and potassium, so keep to one serving; cabbage, peppers and carrot are relatively low-potassium vegetables, and you can leave out the soy sauce.
Diabetes tip: the dish itself is low in carbohydrate; serve it with 1 small whole-wheat flatbread or 100 g brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookinsta (Hani Al-Dosari), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: White Camel Meat Kabsa
description: White camel kabsa is a Najdi dish in which young camel meat (hashi) is boiled with onion and whole spices, without tomato paste, and the rice is cooked in its broth and topped with onion and raisins. This is a home version with 600 g lean meat, leaving out the hump fat and stock cubes and using little ghee and salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean young camel meat (hashi), in large pieces, without hump fat
1 large onion, sliced, for the topping (150 g)
1 small head garlic, whole washed cloves (30 g)
2 tsp ghee (9 g) and 2 tsp olive oil (9 g)
Whole spices: 6 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, ½ tsp black peppercorns, 2 pierced dried black limes
½ tsp ground coriander, and ¼ tsp turmeric for the topping
steps: Put the meat and water in a pot, bring to the boil and skim off the foam as it rises for 10 minutes.
Add the onion quarters, tomato, bell pepper, whole spices and ground coriander, cover and simmer 2–2½ hours until the meat is very tender (or 50–60 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Wash the rice, soak it for 45 minutes, then drain.
Add the salt to the broth, lift out the meat, strain the broth to remove the spices and vegetables, and skim off the fat.
Return the meat to the pot, spread the rice over it and add about 375 ml broth so it sits less than 1 cm above the rice; boil on high heat until the broth is absorbed.
Lay the garlic cloves and chilies on the rice, cover and cook on very low heat for 25 minutes.

For the topping: heat the ghee and oil in a non-stick pan and cook the sliced onion with the turmeric and a splash of water until golden, then add the raisins for 1 minute. Spread over the rice and leave covered for 10 minutes.
Serve the rice on a platter with the meat on top or buried underneath in the traditional way, with green salad.
hints: What changed: no hump fat (traditionally added), lean meat with the fat skimmed off the broth, whole spices instead of a stock cube, and only two teaspoons of ghee for flavour.

Kidney tip: camel meat is rich in protein and phosphorus and raisins are high in potassium; keep to the meat portion (about 100 g cooked) and you can skip the raisins. White kabsa without tomato paste is lower in potassium than the red version.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 56 g carbohydrate; serve with a large green salad, and you can mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Meat and More, Hawaa World
